en: Preface to the Anthology of Verses on the Lotus Land:
The Sūtra states that in the Pure Land, the jeweled trees and pearl nets, the waters of virtue, and the precious birds constantly produce sounds that are clear, refreshing, harmonious, and elegant.
These pervade the world, all expounding the wondrous Dharma; this is because our Tathāgata Amitāyus desires to...
The sound of the Dharma flows forth, and through these miraculous transformations, sentient beings who hear it experience immeasurable joy.
They naturally accord with the path of mindfulness toward heaven, precepts, and renunciation; they naturally accord with the practice of pure detachment from desire;

they naturally accord with the dharmas of the six perfections and myriad practices; and they naturally accord with the power of fearlessness and the unique qualities. Thus, they benefit both themselves and others.
Benefit: Delusions and karma are suddenly eliminated, and all attain the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) regarding unsurpassed bodhi.

During the Wanli era, Guanggui of Yunqi Miaoyi An compiled verses from ancient and modern masters praising the Western Land, exhorting the recitation of the Buddha’s name, and expressing the aspiration for rebirth in the Pure Land.
He categorized and arranged them into the work titled *Verses on the Lotus World*. This is indeed the Pure... [text truncated]
The records of prose literature fill the rafters and exhaust the oxen [in their transport]. What, then, is the purpose of this compilation?

Regarding all poetry that accords with prosodic laws, it is able to permeate one’s innermost being and stir the human spirit, such that one unconsciously finds oneself dancing with hands and stamping with feet—only poetry is thus capable of this.
The intent of the Venerable Master was to transform people through prosody; may we share in this aim.
How much more so for the teaching-body (dharmakāya) of this land, where purity resides in sound;
with the faculty of hearing so exceptionally sharp and the wisdom born of hearing so perfectly complete, what difficulty could there be in transforming this Sahā world into a realm of pure peace?

Elder Xuanyong of the Jingyuan Society collected and supplemented over one hundred additional verses, revised their headings, and titled the work *Selections of Poetry from the Lotus Land*, entrusting me with the preface to its volume. Looking upon my own unworthiness, I am but a weed...

I am incompetent and dare not offer further words of praise. I have briefly gathered together the divine transformations of the Dharma King, the diligent efforts of the Venerable Master, and the great vows of the Elder Xuan, in order to provide a model for my fellow practitioners and to encourage myself as well. Written by the Layman Guyu as the original preface.
Written by Guanggui at Miaoyi Hermitage under the Yunqi Monastery.
The Buddha said: "The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas of all times, are the body of the Dharma-realm; thus, the body that pervades the Dharma-realm is Amitābha Buddha."
What is pure and what is defiled? What is pleasure and what is suffering? However, the *Jingdu sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Pure Deliverance) states:
"When a person gives rise to one thought, they receive one body; with a hundred thoughts, they receive a hundred bodies; with a thousand thoughts, they receive a thousand bodies.

In a single day and night, they plant the roots of birth and death, and hereafter shall receive eight hundred and fifty million bodies of various species. This is the soul-spirit produced within a hundred years."
They undergo suffering according to their respective species throughout the great trichiliocosm; their very bodies, bones, skin, and hair likewise pervade the great trichiliocosm.
When their skin, hair, teeth, and horns manifest in such a dense and terrifying array, how could they possibly know that these various forms throughout the entire dharma-realm are Amitābha Buddha?
When the whips rain down upon them and the knives descend as they are butchered and carved, how could they possibly know?
The various classes of bodies undergoing suffering throughout the entire dharma-realm are Amitābha Buddha.

When one is being boiled in cauldrons, sawed with blades, ploughed by oxen, or scorched by fire, how could one possibly know that the bodies of hungry ghosts and hell-beings suffering throughout the entire dharma-realm are Amitābha Buddha?
Not only is he thus majestic and human-like, but when one encounters the hardships of suffering—suddenly meeting the calamities of war and weapons—[he is present].
At that time, one would be unable to know that this body of ours, suffering such hardship, is Amitābha Buddha.
Not only would one fail to attain immediate joy and satisfaction, with the five desires for one's own amusement and glory filling one's heart;

at that time, one would likewise be unable to know that this body of ours, receiving such enjoyment, is Amitābha Buddha. Indeed, whether in the world there is favor or adversity, [one still cannot perceive it].
If one can know that this body is Amitābha Buddha even now, how much more so at the moment when the "wind-blades" dismember the body and the eight sufferings burn with intensity!

How much more so when one undergoes a transformation of head and face, becoming a creature of feathers, fur, bones, or horns! How much more so on the days of the Flaming Mouth, the needle-throated, the boiling cauldrons, and the molten copper!
After that, would one still not know that one’s own body is Amitābha Buddha? *Vajraśekhara* [Sūtra].
The *Rasavāda-sūtra* records that Mañjuśrī said: "Because all ordinary beings are bound by their own [afflictions], they perceive the signs of hell;
although these do not truly exist, they cause the experiencer to undergo suffering. It is like seeing one's own body falling into hell within a dream."
Burned by ten thousand fires and cast into boiling cauldrons, that person cries out in their dream, "It is extreme suffering!

If one realizes that this is a dream—illusory and unreal—the body and mind attain peace. Thus, the *Fayuan* says: "For one who contemplates the emptiness of the nature of sin, sin arises from the mind;
if the mind were obtainable, sin could not be non-existent. Yet in this dusty world, how many are those whose minds are empty? Dream.
As for those who break [the precepts], how many are there? This is why the Tathāgata teaches people to recite one phrase of "Amitābha Buddha":

it is precisely to encompass their hundreds of thoughts, thousands of thoughts, and eighty-five million miscellaneous thoughts within that single thought-moment. When one reaches this single thought-moment, not even a single thought arises.

One spontaneously realizes and beholds Amitābha Buddha. Thereafter, one knows that the single thought, the hundred thoughts, the thousand thoughts, and the eighty-five million miscellaneous thoughts are all the thought of Amitābha Buddha.

Thereafter, one knows that the single body, the hundred bodies, the thousand bodies, and the eighty-five million bodies of various kinds are all the body of Amitābha Buddha. Thereafter, one knows [the nature of] animals...
Those born in the realms of hungry ghosts and hell are all within the Dharma-realm of Amitābha Buddha. Thus, as the sutra says:
"A single utterance of 'Namo Amitābha Buddha' extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas. Is this not profoundly deep and clearly manifest?
Therefore, know that one utterance of "Namu Amida Butsu" is precisely the testimony that there is neither purity nor defilement in the Pure Land;
it is the testimony that there is neither suffering nor joy in Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī). It is the elixir that empties the mind;
it is the thunderclap amidst a great dream. Alas, we know full well this is a dream, yet we continue to seek within the dream; we know full well this is...
A dream led me into the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa), yet I remained confused and bewildered. How could the roads to one’s native land not be utilized?

The words of those who have passed through this way—those who beckon, advise, support, and nourish one—are essential. Confucius said, "One is aroused by the Odes (Śīkṣā), established by the Rites (Li), and perfected by Music (Yue).

Among these three, it is only the establishment in the Rites that provides the power of steadfastness; yet without being aroused by the Odes and perfected by Music, such steadfastness cannot be achieved.
Thus, from beginning to end, all matters are rendered in verse to evoke joy and melt away rigid defenses. Therefore, within the radiance of the Pure Land,
not only do the sounds emitted by the Tathāgata expound the wondrous Dharma, but even the sound of the mani-water flowing among the flowers proclaims suffering,
emptiness, impermanence, non-self, and the various pāramitās, praising all Buddhas.

The primary and secondary marks [of the Buddha] were radiant; from the king of wish-fulfilling jewels, golden light surged forth, transforming into birds of a hundred precious colors that sang together with harmonious and elegant melodies, constantly praising mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Sangha.
Within the pavilions, the various devas performed celestial music, and musical instruments suspended in mid-air resounded spontaneously without being struck.
Amidst these myriad sounds, all spoke of mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Bhikṣu Saṅgha.
In short, the flowing waters and radiant light, as well as the various jewel-trees, ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks, all preach the wondrous Dharma.

Thus, whether the practitioner is emerging from or entering into meditative concentration, they hear this wondrous Dharma. Even those who sit upon the lotus flowers still rely on these sounds to increase their progress;
how much more so for those who have not yet reached the lotus pond? The *Xiaozhuan* records that when Zhang Zifang was at...

Within the Han army, although Xiang Yu’s forces had been defeated, they still held their own. Zhang Liang then instructed the troops to sing the "Baiyu" (Songs of Chu), causing the men of Chu to long for their hometowns;
thus, the Han cause was ultimately achieved. It can be seen that the way of sound and music can supplement the means of conquest.
This is like the ancient worthies’ hymns to the Pure Land, which are themselves the "Song of Returning Home" by Zhang Liang. Observe this for yourself:
Those who compose verses on the Pure Land have mostly emerged from among the masters of the Chan school; they are truly the "Zi-fang" (Kung-sun Yang) of the Buddhist gate.

The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* records the introduction to the Tathāgata’s great vows: in the past, during his causal stage, Amitābha Buddha was a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), and Śākyamuni Buddha was a minister;
together they made great aspirational vows before the Buddha Ratnagarbha. The universal monarch vowed for a pure and blissful land.
The world is to be gathered in and sustained by sentient beings. Great Minister, you vow to deliver sentient beings within this world of the five turbidities and its afflictions.
Because these vows of the sovereign and his minister are infinite and inexhaustible, the two Tathāgatas became brothers.

While they were śrāmaṇeras, they together used the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to teach and deliver sentient beings; yet, beyond the bestowal of the path through the Three Vehicles, there remain those who have not yet been fully delivered.

Since those to be saved reside with Amitābha, this single gateway of the Pure Land has been brought forth. Through mutual encouragement and support, the transformation of beings through the Way is accomplished.
For this reason, throughout the forty-nine years of his teaching, Śākyamuni Buddha, within the Mahāyāna sūtras he established, constantly took refuge in and returned to this one gateway.
Yet, in this assembly, he repeatedly and earnestly emphasized the single gate of the Pure Land alone;
for instance, regarding the one scroll of the *Amitābha Sūtra* that people recite morning and evening, its phrasing is concise and brief, yet it states once again: "Sentient beings who hear it..."
"One should make a vow: 'May I be born in that land. Furthermore, it says: 'Sentient beings who hear this teaching should make a vow to be born in that land.
And again it says: 'If there are those with faith, they should make a vow to be born in that land.'"
Regarding the statement that the Land of Ultimate Bliss is adorned with such accomplished merits and virtues, there are one, two, three, and four mentions.
The statement that "you, sentient beings, should believe in this *Sūtra on the Inconceivable Merits Protected and Mindfully Regarded by All Buddhas*" appears six times in the Qin translation.
By the time of the Tang translation, following the section where the Buddhas of the ten directions offer praise, [the count changes].
He saw this ten times. Furthermore, he said: "You all must believe and accept my words and those spoken by all the Buddhas.
To savor the tone of these words, one cannot help but feel regret that they did not fill the ears of all sentient beings;
one cannot help but feel regret that they did not penetrate the lungs and intestines of sentient beings. How intense is his love! How profound is his concern! How great is his compassion!
When [the Buddha] arrived, even the most loving parents, when entrusting their children morning and evening, would likely not have been so earnest and urgent.
Why is this? Because worldly parents entrust themselves to their descendants merely with the hope that they will establish a household and build a career;
as for the Tathāgata’s regard for sentient beings, he does not enter through such a gate, for he sees that they must inevitably fall into the boiling cauldrons of hell.
Amidst this boiling cauldron, gain and loss are no small matter; thus, if sentient beings do not recite the Buddha’s name, how could our compassion not be profound?

Sentient beings who recite the Buddha’s name are naturally gathered and never abandoned by him. As the treatise states: "It is like fish eggs and their mother; if the mother does not attend to her offspring, they will rot and perish.
If the Buddha did not attend to sentient beings, their roots of goodness would likewise perish. Therefore, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* says: [and so forth].
He said: "In a future age, when the Way of the sutras has been extinguished, I shall out of compassion specially preserve this sutra so that it remains for another hundred years.
He further stated: "After this sutra has perished, the Buddha-dharma will be entirely gone; only the four-character name of Amitābha Buddha shall remain to save suffering sentient beings.
May the rulers and subjects, brothers and sisters of this world, be able to support one another in the Pure Land and establish a transformation for the masses."
All births flow forth from the great vows of Amitābha and Śākyamuni.
The First Verse on the Western Land of the Tathāgata’s Great Vows. Part One. Introduction.
The Master of Transformation in the West delivers those lost in delusion; through the Buddha’s sustaining power, the Way is easily accomplished.
Letting go of all and proceeding directly, there is no other path—this first step must be clearly understood.
In the Western Land, it is enough simply to resolve the mind with firmness; exert yourself in diligent cultivation to advance swiftly. Like a boat sailing downstream, add oars and paddles;
may the Guide receive you and lead you forward with the rope of his vow.
The West has remained eternally established throughout past and present; the Compassionate Father pities and delivers his children and grandchildren.
Though there are eighty-four thousand distinct paths and gates, the single phrase of Amitābha is honored by all.
The Great Sage of the Western Quarter, King of the Dharma, extends his welcoming hand to lead the deluded masses as he radiates precious light. Unwearied by toil, his great vows are profound;
he constantly traverses the sea of suffering, steering the vessel of compassion.

In the western direction there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who universally delivers all sentient beings from the river of craving. Through the gates of his six and eight vows, the nine grades are opened;
every person may reach that land—do not let the opportunity slip away.
The Great Way of the West is vast and long-enduring; its merit is towering and immeasurable. It was not only Śākyamuni who opened this path;
all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have praised it.
The Compassionate Father in the West is moved by sorrow; he receives the deluded masses and calls them to return. Hasten to personally entrust your essence to the Lotus Throne;
do not cast yourselves into the mundane world to enter a womb.
In the midst of the Pure Land, the peaks, lotuses, and ponds bloom daily;
four-colored radiance reflects upon the jeweled terraces. Your golden arms extend afar as your compassionate mindfulness is most earnest—why do sentient beings not contemplate coming?
The earth shakes and heaven is startled as he diligently recites the Buddha’s name; knocking at gates and beating on doors, he exhorts others to practice. Why does he dig channels in such a manner?
He only fears that sentient beings will fall into the fiery pit.
The ten vows are vast and profound, beyond measure; in every thought and every moment, proclaim them far and wide. Amitābha’s vows shall surely be fulfilled;
four-colored lotus flowers fill the world with fragrance.
The Buddha Amitābha is the King of the Dharma; amidst the waves of the river of craving, he acts as a vessel.
With single-minded resolve, he vows to deliver those submerged in suffering, leading them all to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The Buddhas of the six directions extend their broad and long tongues, together praising those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha in this Sahā world.
One must believe that in the White Lotus World, there is never a time when the springtime of the kalpa-jar does not flourish.
Praise to Amitābha Buddha, the Teacher of the Pure Land: His name is Amitābha; with forty-eight vows, he benefits the Sahā world. May all beings of the nine grades ascend to the other shore;
May he deliver all sentient beings from the river of craving.
The verse says: With objectless compassion, he gathers in sentient beings—how wondrous!
The plum blossoms have fallen away, and the apricot flowers bloom. How could it be that the spring breeze blows with deliberate intent? The single breath speaks not, yet it contains all forms;
Where among the myriad spirits can one thank its impartiality?
Each and every ray of light universally illumines the worlds of the ten directions; it gathers in and does not abandon those sentient beings who mindfully recite the Buddha’s name.
Within the shadow of the silent light, the entire body appears. The light pervading all realms stands far beyond compare; like fish in warm waves remembering the peach blossoms.
My son, with无缘慈 (unconditioned compassion) you deliver those with缘 (conditions);
a single point of compassionate heart cannot be split open. Amidst the boiling cauldrons, your smile fills your cheeks. This rare and marvelous matter I, the Emperor, believe deeply;
see how you come to preach the Dharma for the Sovereign.
Eulogy on the Image of Amitābha by Shen Zhītáng:
When hungry, it is food; when thirsty, it is tea and soup; when ill, it is medicine; when naked, it is clothing. [It delivers one] from the boundless sea of suffering.

They are transformed into bridges and rafts. In the dark chamber of ignorance, the light of a lamp illuminates the way. When the road is exhausted and the day draws to a close, one returns to one's hometown.
Amidst the scorching heat of a blazing sky, a cool breeze blows forth. Fire, water, thieves, and robbers—these evils do not obstruct one another; nor do the venomous vipers, snakes, and scorpions.
Poisons cannot harm them; they encounter people and deliver them, bringing auspicious blessings wherever they go. They are the compassionate father, the king of great vows.

Human life is as fleeting as a breath; impermanence is swift. May our hearts be sealed with one another, never forgetting this from moment to moment, so that we may transcend to the highest grade of rebirth.

Sitting securely upon the Compassionate Vessel, one is reborn in the lower grade of the Pure Land, which is yet superior to the heavens. With hands extended downward, he receives and guides us all to the Western Land.
He earnestly exhorts us to turn back from the path of suffering; the Buddha says:
"Those who obtain a human body are like the soil upon a fingertip; those who lose a human body are like the soil upon the earth. Although one has faith...

The Buddha spoke, yet its reason was not yet understood. Upon reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it says: "The karmic actions created by the six consciousnesses of all sentient beings result in retributions for evil that emerge from the six sense organs.
Those who fully commit evil karma through all six organs enter the Avīci Hell; those who create [evil] through each of the six organs individually [enter other hells]."

Regarding those who commit offenses involving both objects and faculties: they enter eighteen hells for committing killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct through the three actions of body, speech, and mind.
Those whose three karmas do not involve all [faculties] enter thirty-six hells. Those who violate a single faculty alone enter one hundred and eight hells.
Within the hells, one is scorched for kalpas; only when the retribution for one's sins is exhausted does one receive the form of a hungry ghost.

Once the karma of a ghost is finished, one then encounters the original debtor from the world as an adversary, taking the form of an animal to repay past debts. Thus, the duration of these three miserable realms is as vast as this.
Regarding the calculation of lifespans as recorded in the sutras, the lifespan in the hells is such that one day and night in the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva) compares to—
According to human calculation, sixteen thousand two hundred *koṭis* of years pass as one advances further through the hells.

Such is the length of life in a single realm of hell. Thus, when a spiritual friend says that once one loses this human body, it will be difficult to emerge from it for ten thousand *kalpas*, what time span could they possibly mean?
Is this not a statement made with a heart carved open and entrails torn asunder?

These are words spoken with tears streaming down in bitter lamentation! In this world today, among those who seek the purity of their six sense faculties, how many are there who do not transgress even a single precept?
Thus, in this vast and boundless secular world, for the most part, everything is but a cause for the hells.

If one seeks to be reborn as a hungry ghost or an animal, such a thing is still impossible to achieve; how can one not feel a cold dread at heart? In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it records [the case of] an animal...
In the midst of birth, one must repay karmic retributions by spending money and exerting labor; once these are fully settled, one’s state ceases.

However, if one takes another's life or eats their flesh, one will undergo mutual devouring and slaughter for as many eons as there are motes of dust, alternating between being the superior and the inferior without respite.
Such is the transmigration resulting from eating meat. Therefore, if we were to lose this very face and body of ours even once, what would we become when reborn?
For years. All such sufferings as these cannot be seen by ourselves with our ordinary eyes; only the Tathāgata knows them all and sees them all.
How could he not speak with earnestness and urgency, using a thousand words and ten thousand phrases, speaking with bitter words to others?

It is truly pitiable that those who do not recite the Buddha’s name during their daily lives are unable to recite it even amidst the agonies of hell. Recently, there have been instances of those who were revived...
King Yama commands the denizens of hell to recite the Buddha’s name; yet, even if they can but recite a single phrase of "Amitābha Buddha," he immediately releases them from prison.
However, their mouths are clenched so that they cannot utter a single word of "Buddha. Such is the gravity of the obstacle of a lack of faith.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There are bodhisattvas who, reflecting upon themselves, realize that by slandering the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, they have fallen into the evil realms and will remain there for immeasurable kalpas.

Although they may practice other deeds, they cannot extinguish their transgressions. Later, encountering a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), they are instructed to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha;
only then can they eliminate their obstacles and be reborn transcendentally in the Pure Land. Thus, we who are sentient beings within the ocean of karma [must likewise rely on this method]."
Aside from the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha," where else could one find a livelihood?
This is an earnest exhortation to turn back the reins, the second warning to the world: *Bhadra*.
Failing to form auspicious karmic bonds with the virtuous, you suffer from greed for fame and profit, tormented day and night.
How could you know that the gold, silver, and treasures in this world were lent to you for your idle viewing over several decades?
A Warning to the World:
Drawn by the desire for kāma, one continues to sink until the end of time. Afflictions arise daily and follow one constantly. In the government prisons, there is still hope for pardon;
but when one is bound by the constraints of household affairs, there is no time for pardon.
A Warning to the World:

Half-relying on the earth, water, fire, and wind elements, this body is transformed; when the body perishes, the four great elements each return to their source. All demons and the six thieves are utterly dispersed;
suffering and joy in the future are merely the guest of the host.
Exhortation to Practice Nianfo (Buddha-Recitation) by Shandao:
Gradually, the skin becomes like that of a rooster and the hair like that of a crane; look at how the gait grows faltering and unsteady.

Even if gold and jade fill the halls, one cannot escape decay, decrepitude, old age, and illness. No matter how many kinds of pleasures you may enjoy, when the time of impermanence finally arrives, there is only the direct path.
In practicing cultivation, simply keep the Buddha Amitābha in mind.
As an ancient poem by Páng Dàoxuán says:
"Year after year, one's efforts are merely to delay; the skin wrinkles and the complexion fades, the hair turns white and the marrow dries up."
The pores allow wind to pass through; the bones are as fragile as rafters and eaves. Water is slight and cannot endure heat; fire is meager and cannot withstand cold.
This illusory body is like a mass of foam; the four great elements are likewise not solid. Yet it is further driven by delusion and cruelty, tormented day and night by ignorance.
One knows only to mind water and grass, while the spirit and mind are entangled by external things. Why do you not repent? You merely speak of discarding wealth and money;
with such superficial, evasive words, you hope to escape your prior transgressions. The hells will surely have no peace for you, yet you calculate that you shall be reborn in heaven.
In the world there are such beings; it is not so in the realm of the dead. Unless one ceases to create karma, one must uproot the source of transgression.
When the root is empty and the objects are unreal, internal and external causes and conditions are severed. Though accumulated sins are like mountain peaks, the fire of wisdom burns them all at once.
In a mere instant it turns to ash; for eternal kalpas, not even smoke remains.
Behold the diagrams of hell: how piercing!
These towering peaks are no mere Jianke Pass. There are trees, yet who could dare to climb them? Even the Buddha’s hand cannot shield one; the human heart seems so indifferent.
The King of Zhou has yet to clear his name; what face can Bai Qi show? All day long he vainly snaps his fingers within this bustling world of dust.
A Compassionate Warning to the World:
Those who fish cannot hunt; those who hunt cannot fish. But for the wealthy, money serves as their net, capable of ensnaring both creatures of water and land.

Having tasted every kind of animal flesh, the hearts of the Buddhas have grown increasingly distant. The path to the Yellow Springs is slippery; should one lose their footing, it will be difficult to support them.
Furthermore, the mind gives rise to greed for fine food and anger toward coarse food. Chattering away until satiated, they remain utterly unaware of where such things come from.
In the space of a single meal in this life, greed, anger, and delusion are all fully present. Let the wise reflect well; do not err for the sake of a mere mouthful of food.
I exhort the assembly to practice mindfulness of the Buddha:
look at these hair and brows, already dyed by snow and frost; the mind-monkey and will-horse remain wild and unruly. One day, when the eyes are closed, one returns to emptiness.
Depart! Only now do you begin to believe that the years and months in the hells are long.
Karmic retributions vary and circumstances differ; in this weary life, there is no place to escape the cage.
If you wish to know the Amitābha Buddha of your own nature, look for him within a single thought-moment of your daily morning and evening.
It is not that this mountain monk is priding himself on discerning right from wrong; you must understand that these are the demonic obstacles encountered in practice.
You must simply tighten the soles of your straw sandals and pass through the pool of the five desires of this Sahā world.
Warning on the Inferior Class:
In the silent and foolish stream, the practice of evil has long become a prevailing custom. Throughout one's life, how could one have known the tracks of black and white karma?

Only when death approaches and all karmic deeds manifest do they finally realize, with alarm, that they are besieged by the four snakes. Were it not for the power of past roots of goodness and the force of hearing the Dharma, how could one be called "brave"?
A Mighty Merit! Suddenly one perceives a cool breeze blowing upon the fires of karma. Within the light of the jade-hair radiance is the golden countenance.
Praise to the Pure Land:
amidst the four-colored lotus flowers on the northern mountain, green lotus leaves intermingle. Upon each lotus flower sits one Amitābha; do not doubt the journey to the Pure Land.
How far we are from the truth! Day by day, the raindrops of human life fall thick and fast;
the evening drum and the morning cock ceaselessly urge us on. In a mere moment, our appearance changes, growing frail and decrepit.
Do not say that white hair is a trivial matter; it is all the arrival of the message of impermanence.
Verse One from the West:
The ultimate truth of the Western Paradise—believe it with sincerity and do not give rise to doubt. The practice of Buddha-recitation requires that one act while there is still time.
This finite lifespan should be used to prepare early; how many know that skulls will soon lie upon the ground?
In the West lies a path few ascend; the single phrase "Amitābha" is the Supreme Vehicle. One cannot lead another by the hand;
only when one is self-accepting does it accord with the Way.
Return early to your native land in the West; human life is impermanent, lasting but a breath. Cherish this finite time;
once you have wasted this present life, it will be difficult to emerge again.
Hasten in the West and practice early; birth and death are impermanent and cannot be anticipated.
The sunlight outside the window passes in the blink of an eye—how much time does one have as a human being?
Step by step in the West, one treads upon lotus flowers; pointing the way and opening the gate, I take leave of Śākyamuni. Repeated three times with earnest sincerity, there is no other teaching:
with single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha, return home early.
The Western Land is easy to practice through direct pointing; who among us knows their own original nature as Amitābha?
Wandering through the six realms and three miserable paths of birth and death—how can one contemplate this without feeling pain and sorrow?
The Western Land is easy to reach and accessible for practice; with ten focused recitations, one shall be reborn there. I exhort all people, men and women alike:
let us all hasten together to complete our journey home.
The merit of the Western Land is equal to that of the heavens; yet those who slander Amitābha are icchantikas.
Having fallen into hell for immeasurable kalpas, one knows not when these deluded masses will awaken.
Not reaching the Western Land is indeed difficult; once one loses this human body, it is as hard as pulling up a mountain with bare strength. Entrust this to the heroic and spirited men of the world:
you must urgently gather the treasure and not return empty-handed.
In the Pure Land Verse:

"Peak after peak, kalpa after kalpa, and yet more kalpas like the sands of the Ganges; though one counts these kalpas until their end, one does not cease. One should reflect that this is solely because one has not cast off worldly passions;
thus, one remains bound by boundless birth and death."
The four great elements coalesce to form the horns of a phantom hare; the six sense organs bind one to the hair of a white tortoise.
Performing somersaults amidst bubbles and reflections, how many times have you appeared and vanished within this Jambudvīpa?
A single bright red ball in the eastern sea; its flowing light shoots daily toward the western grove. How many extraordinary men are there in this world?
Who, at their window, treasures every moment of time?
When the pool of blood dries up, the lotus pond becomes clear; when the sword-trees wither, the jewel-trees flourish. Suffering and pleasure originally possess no abiding characteristic;
within this state of non-abiding, they are spontaneously perfected.
The Buddha and sentient beings have shared a karmic affinity since time immemorial; the Buddha-nature within sentient beings is impartial.
Why, then, do you willingly endure the sufferings of this Sahā world, refusing to turn back and accept the lash of pain?
Among humans, in the heavens, and in the hells—how long have I been laboring through this cycle of ascent and descent?
If the white lotus has roots but they are not planted, one will remain bound by the sands of birth and death.
Within one's own home is a single Amitābha Buddha; throughout kalpas, when has he ever been seen with the eyes? Today, one turns further with sounds and forms;
this time, if one wishes to see him, it will be difficult.

The affairs of the five human desires are boundless; the iron shackles of profit and the reins of fame cannot be severed. If you take the mind that seeks profit and fame and instead recite the Buddha’s name, why must you toil in hardship awaiting the future?
Reflect deeply on the hells and give rise to bodhicitta. Do not remain deluded regarding your parents or your homeland. Lash yourself with the whip of pain and strive to arrive early;
do not let the sun shift to the west before you have reached your goal.
In the seventh month, the human world’s heat gradually wanes; the evening breeze by the pond is even more agreeable.
Gazing afar at the setting sun like a suspended drum, I already find my urging of the homeward whip too late.
The year’s end has come; how pitiable are these worldly affairs. Old Wang of the eastern village burns paper money at night.
The Buddha Amitābha is one's own mind and nature; yet another year passes with a face covered in dust.
I send these words to the people of this Sahā world: if you seek the path home, do not be complacent.
Once you have pierced through the silver mountains and iron walls, the thousand-petaled lotus will be a spring of its own.
Reciting the Buddha's name never obstructs daily life; it is people who obstruct one another in their daily activities. Who can guarantee this illusory shadow of a hundred-year life?
Do not fail the Great Vow-King from the Western Heaven.

Those who possess wealth and honor should properly practice mindfulness of the Buddha. Though their treasuries are filled with gold and their granaries overflowing with grain, and though they lack nothing for worldly enjoyment, they remain deficient in one thing alone:
seeing the King of Vows at the moment of death.
When a person of humble means recites the Buddha’s name, they have no household affairs to occupy their thoughts.
Bare-bodied and with empty hands, they ascend directly to the lotus pedestal and claim a single branch.
In old age, reciting the Buddha's name is most appropriate; with few days remaining, do not forget it for even a moment.
The six characters "Namo Amitābha" are called the compassionate vessel that crosses the sea of suffering.
The world at large says it is difficult for the young to practice mindfulness of the Buddha; I say that youth is precisely the right time.
Behold the Dragon King’s daughter at eight years of age, who held a divine pearl in her palm and radiated precious light.
Having served as a high minister and a court official, your worldly fame and merit were beyond measure.
Yet if you do not contemplate the Amitābha of your own nature, I know not how you can withstand impermanence.
First-rate masters constantly advise others that if one does not apply oneself diligently to the samādhi of one’s own mind, though one may dwell in the pure land of white lotuses,
one is merely emptying one's lips by reciting the name of Amitābha.
In the realm of universal equality where all is but mind, noble and base, wise and foolish, are no two paths. We must teach even the lacquer bucket to be emptied to its very bottom;
let everyone apply their efforts together.
He has already attained Buddhahood this very morning; the Master of the Land of Bliss has already deemed it too late. How can you still wish to linger?
Take it for granted that your cycle of rebirth will have no end.
Four snakes in a single basket—peril upon peril; two rats gnawing at a vine—danger upon danger.
If one does not plant the lotus in the pure realm, who knows when this kalpa will find its end?
All sufferings arise from craving; one does not know that craving arises from nowhere else than from forgetting the self-nature of Amitābha Buddha.
When divergent thoughts run wild, they are all nothing but demons.
The river of craving is vast and boundless; the mooring ropes of the six sense faculties must be firm and strong.
Bind the mind single-mindedly to the shore of Bodhi, and lift your steps to ascend the vessel of Prajñā.
A warning to the world:
three libations poured, then another three; a single skull remains unburnt. The karmic consciousness has already burrowed back into its skin-sack;
even an iron man would find his hair standing on end at this.
A Stone to Warn the World:

When rain has passed over the thatched eaves, the sun shines red. In an instant, the weather changes from gloom to clarity; how much more so the matter of life and death, which occurs in the space of a breath?
At twilight, one can hardly guarantee reaching the morning bell.

Verses on Exhorting the World to Practice Buddha-Recitation (Anonymous) The karmic enemies of killing gradually multiply their debts; with what words or reasoning can one face King Yama? I teach you a single path for transcending rebirth:
it is better to recognize your faults and repent, and recite the name of Amitābha.
Exhortation to Practice Buddha-Recitation:
Utpala, life and death are a frantic bustle at the ancient ferryhead. Amitābha nudges forth the boat that ferries beings across.
If you had the karmic affinity in past lives, you meet it now; Quickly board the ship and depart to rest.
A single thought of delusion gives rise to ten thousand ends; the defiled karma-consciousness rolls into a solid mass.
Were one not a man of fierce and heroic spirit, it would be difficult indeed to break through and emerge from its head.
I recite the name of Amitābha without seeking Zen; I merely seek a quick tongue to gain the upper hand.
Fortunately, I possess a nose that reaches the heavens, yet it has been pierced by the child of ignorance and karma.
When old age arrives and death is imminent, how can one be cured? Who knows the splendor of that Land of Bliss? Those who reach it are all named Amitāyus;
for this reason, recite the name of Amitābha within this world.
The Dharma-body is pure and fundamentally free from dust; yet, alas, sentient beings create the causes of karma.
They willingly endure suffering in the hells and the three miserable paths, their clear principles never having been vindicated.
Awakened to this truth, I look back at my discarded remains piled up like mountains; tears of parting overflow like the waves of the four seas. This world will ultimately meet its end in destruction;
in the blink of an eye, what joy is there in human life? Having been born as male and female a thousand times over, one has donned horns and shed fur through countless lifetimes.
Ten thousand complications arise. If you do not take birth in the Pure Land in this very life, it will be difficult to repent once you have made the error of entering a womb.
Verse on Reciting the Buddha’s Name (Extensive):
You must fix your eyes upon the Buddha within your own heart; Do not cast him behind your head and fail to look upon him. If you miss this moment, you will truly fall into ruin.
Mistaken! It seems that today will bring great peril.
*Wang Jiangnan* (Gazing South of the River):
"The Sahā world is suffering; our lives are like a single floating duckweed. Moths and gnats struggle for petty gain upon the tips of eyelashes; snails and slugs steal at the points of cow horns."
Empty fame; a single spark of resentment is hard to settle. The "self" and "other" are rampant; day and night, ignorance grows ever longer.
At the very end of hell, one falls further down. In the Western Paradise, not a single person is willing to practice. Empty death, followed by empty birth once more.
The suffering of this Sahā world is like light and shadow, rushing away like a flowing stream. When will honor and disgrace, sorrow and joy, come to an end?
When will right and wrong, self and other, cease to be? The path of birth and death is long and vast; within the three realms, we are but a single bubble upon the water.
Even if a hero’s achievements cover the world, they leave nothing but white bones buried in a desolate grave. Why not turn back early?
In the Pure Land of Chu, even a youth turns old and withers in an instant;
one must believe that impermanence urges on day and night. Through the false wisdom of the ninety-six schools, one undergoes saṃsāra for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
If one does not maintain the visualization of the jeweled realm and the lotus pond, how can one avoid the mountain of knives and swords?
The tree has fallen; yet from a mind purified by itself, one attains the Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī). Herein, the sages and worthies permit one’s company.
Having lost the human body beneath the Buddha’s *kāṣāya*, how many are there who regain it again? Ten thousand practices are not equal to cultivating pure deeds (*śukla-karman*).
Why, with a single mind, suffer such attachment to the red dust of the world? The Dharma King’s vow is as heavy as a mountain; the lost son longs to return, his tears flowing.
Tears flow incessantly. If you could understand how to reflect inwardly and contemplate your own nature, then whatever is cast away or discarded would be nothing but your own precious treasure.

Those born in this Saha world are utterly deluded; entangled by myriad sufferings, they do not understand to reflect. While in this life, they possess no further pure karma; at the moment of death, how could there be a time of liberation?
Among hundreds of thousands of sutras, there is earnest exhortation; yet among ten billion people, there is but one [who understands].
Second, the knowledge [of impermanence]: O Great Sage of Golden Arms, come quickly and lead me into the lotus pond.
Even in the midst of busyness, one must steal moments of leisure; who among men can fulfill a hundred years of spring?

Parting and welcoming never cease; sorrow and joy burn within us, renewing day by day. Cease thinking of fame and office, and contemplate only the Buddha; concern yourself solely with the path of practice, and do not—
Anxiety over poverty suddenly blossoms upon the iron tree. The Tathāgata’s sublime turning of the True Dharma Wheel:
the great affliction is manifest because there is a body. One must know that illness spares no one; it is merely a matter of delusive thoughts, all of which are false.
Even if one attains the status of a true immortal, this is not yet the ultimate reality. As the masses of heat gather, the wind fans the fire; at the end of one's term, the bones are cast away.
The sinews are bound tight; only the recitation of the Buddha’s name can liberate one from birth and death.

To cling only to Jambudvīpa is to turn oneself into dust. No crime is as heavy as killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; the body is imprisoned in the penal cell while the mouth groans in pain. Even if shackles are struck and chains are beaten, one must be able to invoke the Buddha’s name.

Whether the earth is overturned or heaven is turned upside down, do not let your mind change. Let the ghosts and spirits howl at midnight as they may; there is a Sage naturally present within the void.
The worthy one approaches; gathering causes and bearing fruit upon the lotus pedestal, the Amitābha of one's own nature need not be sought elsewhere.
A poem on the Pure Land:
With lofty talent, expansive strategy, and extraordinary spirit, who would fail to remain composed when the moment arrives? When rain lashes and wind beats, what plan shall we devise?

Compared to this, those writings that startle heaven and shake the earth are but empty rhetoric. As long as the River of Love has not been dried up and exhausted, one must still take the initiative amidst its shallow waves.
The six characters of Amitābha require no commentary; taking refuge in them is itself the Great Compassionate Vessel.
Exhorting the practice of the Pure Land, Xueqiao gave instructions to the boatman steering the vessel:
"You must recognize the waves of the long river, both flowing with and against the current. I only fear that a favorable wind might blow you past the fire;
once you have turned back, it will be difficult as the headwinds are many."
The verse says: "In the lower grade, one is born in the middle [lotus] with excellence.

(Regarding those born in the middle of the lower grade: when their life is about to end, the various fires of hell arrive all at once. They encounter a virtuous friend who instructs them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha to be reborn in the West. After six kalpas, the lotus flower opens; Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma. As for those born in the lower [of the lower grade]:)

Upon the end of his life, he should have undergone suffering for kalpas; however, having encountered a spiritual friend who revealed to him the ten recitations for rebirth in the Pure Land, twelve great kalpas passed as the lotus flower blossomed and the Bodhisattva preached the Dharma.
The meeting of those with true knowledge is not easily found. How perilous is this bubble upon the waves of the sea!
At the moment when the setting sun is about to fall but has not yet fallen, all is but the sorrow of parting for people of every age.
By invoking the name of the Buddha, in every thought-moment, one eliminates the sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death;
even as iron dogs and copper snakes fiercely brandish their wrath, and the wind-blades and fire-saws reduce the flesh to dust, a single utterance of the Buddha’s name causes one to turn over.
Departing, I turn my head back, yet never see the person of old.
The rooster crows as the moonlight shines bright upon the thatched inn. The traveler’s dream remains mired and has not yet awakened; when the eyes open, the sky is already broad with dawn.
With disheveled hair and soiled face, one rushes toward the path ahead.
It is this very mind-consciousness that creates hell; it is this very mind-consciousness that sees the Buddha and attains Buddhahood.
One falls because of the ground and arises because of the ground. To seek to arise apart from the ground is illogical.
Without leaving the turbid water and the mud, emerging with one's head above is still the lotus ground.
General Summary: Through the causes of attaining roots of goodness in three or many lifetimes of the lower grade, one fortunately escapes the sorrows of the boundless ocean of suffering.
Had I known early on that one sits through entire great kalpas, I would have regretted not having practiced with vigor in this Sahā world.
Pure Land Verses by Ouyi:
The Western Land is precisely the land of the mind alone; Only when conditions are complete can the true cause be realized. Patience and wisdom mutually support one another to perfect the precepts;
This bright pearl is precious—do not treat it with levity.
The Western Land is precisely the realm of Mind-only. To have failed to reach the West is deeply perilous. Past karmic obstructions already surge like billowing waves;
how can one endure new karma following in their wake?
The Western Land is precisely the realm of Mind-only. Only when compassion and wisdom are in accord can it be brought forth. Do not say that Great Compassion should merely pity the turbid world;
to transform others, one must first achieve success through one's own merit.
The Western Quarter is precisely the land of Mind-Only. Within samādhi, the royal path is most subtle; a fleeting doubt arises and one is separated by a thousand ages.
Bite through the nails and chew through the iron—do not waver or compromise.
Verses on Cherishing the Pure Land: The lotus blooms;
conceal the mind and joyfully head toward the Land of Bliss. Do not wait for impermanence to urge you on with old age and sickness.

If you allow this present life to slip away once more, it will be difficult to escape eternal cycles of saṃsāra. Diligently practice the contemplation of the setting sun at the horizon; do not grasp at the world’s empty flowers.
Planting [the seeds] of practice, advance directly in every thought-moment without retreat or fear. Sit by the jeweled pond watching a single lotus bloom;
as the crescent moon and the bell-chimes herald the breaking dawn, how can you still sleep soundly with your head on high? Look back at the days of bamboo horses and kites in the wind;
suddenly one arrives at the age when the head is bald and the teeth are gone. Do not follow the worldly waves into dark karma; quickly recite the Buddha’s name to nurture yourself.
Blue Lotus: You who would go to the Land of Bliss must go now; do not wait for another to take your hand and lead you.
I urge you to practice mindfulness of the Buddha;

at Shen Zhītáng, one cannot escape the cycle of birth and death. In this weary toil, when will there be rest? I urge you to practice mindfulness of the Buddha early; this very moment is the turning back of the head.
The wealthy and noble, the poor and lowly—human life’s conditions differ. All things come to an end; yet the merit of reciting the Buddha's name is inexhaustible.
Stealing a moment of leisure amidst busyness, everyone is capable of this practice. Its efficacy will be verified at the moment of death, when a lotus pedestal awaits in the Pure Land.
Turning with eager longing toward this, the Preface by the Ancient Virtuous One states:
"Sentient beings dwelling in the world of the five turbidities are like prisoners in a jail. Although their offenses may be light or heavy, there is not a single person who does not suffer.
Now, the sufferings of the hells and the hungry ghosts are said to belong to another realm and have not yet..."
This is understood. The suffering of animals is still said to be "separated by the womb," thus remaining unknown.

The sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, death, separation from the beloved, and meeting with the hated are still said to be "the vicissitudes of human life," which do not necessarily occur at all times.

Even if one merely dwells in constancy and complies with circumstances within the confines of the family, what flavor of interest is there? The *Fayuan* cites the statement of the *Vibhāṣā* regarding the home: [it is a place of confinement].
The reasons why dwelling in the household life is utterly loathsome are explained in great detail; here, I shall briefly summarize one or two points. It is said:

"The household is difficult to satisfy, like the ocean swallowing rivers. The household is insatiable, like fire consuming fuel. The household is of the nature of suffering, like an enemy feigning friendship.

The household is strife and discord, characterized by mutual antagonism and contention. The household abounds in anger, censuring the beautiful and the ugly. The household is like a performer, [displaying] all manner of [deceptions]."
Falsely adorning it, one finds that the household is like a dream seen in the eye; once wealth and status are lost, it vanishes. The household is like the morning dew, perishing in an instant.
The household is like a thicket of thorns, seeking to pierce and wound the person. This is the flavor experienced by all in this world who possess bodies and households.
Is this so, or is it not? Therefore, the *Yaoji* cites the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, saying: "Life at home is cramped and confined, like a prison;
all afflictions arise because of it. Only by shaving one's hair and donning the black robes can one be free from such entanglements."
An ancient worthy said: "If one's mind is enlightened as a monk, one has surpassed all others; if that mind is enlightened, is one not a truly transcendent great man?
If it is not enlightened, how does one differ from the laity? Moreover, one's transgressions are even more subtle. This is the resolution of doubts regarding sin and merit.
Regarding matters of money, grain, causes, and effects as set forth in the sutras and treatises:

for instance, if a donor intends to commission a statue of Śākyamuni but instead commissions one of Amitābha, or intends to produce a "Great Sutra" but instead produces the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the offense is calculated based on the amount of money involved. Zhuang Chun stated:

"For every single coin misappropriated from the monastic community (sangha), the interest accrues at three fen and seven li per day and night; on the second day and night," [the interest continues to grow].
The interest is long-term; it is effectively an interest of three parts for every seven cents, compounded by further interest.
In a future life, one must repay this as an ox or a horse. An ox repays eight cash per day, and a horse repays seven cash per day. Thus it is said:
"What is easy in one lifetime becomes a hardship for ten thousand kalpas. Inferring from this, should those who are monks not be struck with trepidation and fear?
Thus, by examining from the left and probing from the right, there is only the single gate of the Pure Land through which one may escape at will;
once departed, there shall never again be a law for dwelling in Jambudvīpa.
Furthermore, in the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses*, the Buddha said: "Incalculable kalpas ago, I was originally an ordinary person.

Since first seeking the path to Buddhahood, I have received bodies within the five destinies through immeasurable births and deaths. Were one to calculate my former bodies, they could not be numbered. Such is the case for Śākyamuni Buddha."

Even after studying the Buddha-dharma, one cannot yet avoid the five realms of existence; how much more so for those who study other paths? Only those born in the Pure Land are certain not to regress.
If one merely upholds the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and gives rise to the aspiration to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha, Śākyamuni Buddha grants them non-retrogression.
Thus, the benefits of this Dharma gate within the path of the Buddha are [immeasurable].
Furthermore, because it is the most supreme, an ancient master said: "Those who cultivate the Pure Land should make this vow:
'Since beginningless time, I have never upheld this Dharma-gate; for this reason, I have transmigrated through the six realms of existence and have not attained liberation.'"
Today I have come to know this. How could I be unwilling to take action immediately?
Instead, I turn my aspirations toward the third Pure Land.
(From "A Poem of Gratitude for the Pure Land" by Xie Lingyun)
Dharmākara grew up within the royal palace; cherishing the Way, he departed from the capital city. He made forty-eight vows, his great aspirations to rescue all living beings.
How wondrous is that Pure Land! Those who come there are all the elite. As my declining years seek a place of rest, I shall follow the transformation of nature and set out on my journey at dawn.
While ill, I paint this transformation tableau of the Western Paradise,
praying that the Pure Land of Sukhāvatī in the Fragrant Mountain (Xiangshan) be free of all evil realms and manifold sufferings.
May those like my own body who endure the pain of illness be reborn together with me in the presence of Amitāyus Buddha.
Seeing Master Zhen off, Li Shangyin wrote:
Lost in the bitter sea of suffering, one has not yet found the way out. How many atoms of dust have passed since leaving the East?
When shall we, upon ten billion lotus flowers, Behold the Buddha’s body within each and every blossom?
Painting of an Image of Amitābha Buddha with Praising Verses by Su Dongpo and the Dharma Master Yuanzhao of Qiantang.
Universally exhorting both monastics and laypeople to take refuge with sincere devotion in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
Su Shi of Meishan respectfully donated the hairpins and earrings—the personal belongings left behind by his deceased mother, Lady Cheng of Shu Commandery—and commissioned an artisan...
Hu Xi painted an image of Amitābha Buddha to dedicate merit for the deceased, composing a verse in praise that said:
"The Buddha, with his great perfect enlightenment, fills the worlds of the ten directions; I, through inverted perceptions, come and go within birth and death."
How can one attain rebirth in the Pure Land through a single thought-moment? Though I have created karma since beginningless time, it all finds its end in a single thought-moment.
Since I am born from a single thought-moment, I likewise perish through a single thought-moment. At the place where birth and death are utterly extinguished, I am identical with the Buddha.
Like water cast into the ocean, like bellows blown by the wind, even with the great wisdom of a Sage, one cannot discern [the difference].
May my former parents and all sentient beings find the West wherever they are, and may all they encounter be the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Every person is Amitāyus; there is neither going nor coming.
A Vow Verse (at the time of death):
Birth and death are like the bending and stretching of an arm. Our hearts are moved by this bitterness for our own kind. To rejoice in heaven is not the same as reaching Penglai.
Guest: Relying upon the West as my host, I offer this long verse on exhorting the cultivation of the Pure Land.
The three realms are blazing like a mass of fire; for the practitioner, they are not yet a place of rest. In the lotus pond, superior friends await many.
At this time, gather your body and mind and return home with care;
let your eyes behold and your heart dwell upon the holy forms. You must maintain this moment by moment without giving rise to doubt;
when the flowers bloom in the Pure Land in years to come, you will remember the time you recited the Buddha’s name here in Saha.
Verse One: Chanting on the Western Land The Western Land is easy to reach;
do not hesitate. It requires only that you cultivate a heart of resolve. With a single snap of the fingers, one transcends the sea of birth and death;
if there is the karmic affinity, one meets it like a mustard seed meeting the eye of a needle.
The path to the Western Land is excellent for practice; with courageous diligence, hasten your progress. All have their share in the nine grades of lotus pedestals;
whether the flowers bloom early or late, one awakens to non-arising.
In the West, take up this one practice without delay. Shake off your lethargy and press forward with vigor. Do not wait until you are parched with thirst before digging a well;
you should simply hasten to board the white lotus boat while there is still time.

Exert yourselves with diligence in the West; do not delay. Once you fall into the City of Doubt for five hundred years, the Great Sage will emit light to illuminate and shatter it, so that you may return once more to the Pure Land and pay homage to the Golden Immortal.

Cultivate diligently early in the west; strike through all right and wrong with a single stroke. Letting go of body and mind while zealously reciting the Buddha’s name, there will be neither affliction nor sorrow.
Pure Land Verse by Xu Zixin:
Relying together on the power of Amitābha, We board the boat of expedient means as one. The Land of Bliss is easily reached; It is truly superior to arduous Zen meditation.

Verse for Rebirth: Ms. Feng (Faxin) For many years, I have followed conditions and been subject to karma, Uselessly acting as an old ox to till the fields. Now, having settled my body and mind, I shall depart early;
May I avoid letting my nostrils be pierced by others.
Within the Pure Land of my heart, at dawn and at dusk, I perform prostrations and repentance.
Bowing my head, I weep and address the Elder Amitābha: "How many times have I wandered through the six realms?
I vow that this time, I shall escape the net."
Exhortation to Practice Nianfo:
In the human realm, the four signs of change make death unavoidable; Even in the heavens, how could one ever escape the five signs of decay?
It would be better to dwell in the lower grade of the nine lotus realms Than to return to this floating world and undergo birth from a womb.
To attain longevity, one need not rely on the formulas of the immortals; to relieve urgent distress, one must require the prescriptions from the Sea of Medicine.
Relying upon the Lord Amitāyus, it turns out that this is far superior to any other considerations.
How many stumble and flee across Jambudvīpa? Worldly affairs are as thick as hemp seeds, growing denser by the day. The fields and gardens of one’s native land lie buried in weeds;
when will the wild ox roam freely come to rest?
Meditating on the Pure Land, Chu Shi-yi wanders alone like a tumbleweed from the south of Jambudvīpa. Leaning against the tower, he sighs longingly as the moon grows slender;

he knows afar that the assembly of Dharma is surrounded by devas, and he visualizes the lotus pedestal adorned with a hundred jewels. This world is like a fish in scant water; this fragile life is but like a swallow’s.
Nesting in the eaves; may my virtuous companions hold me in their hearts. A stupa has been built, yet it lacks its pinnacle.
A poem on the Pure Land:
beneath the forest trees of Mount Xueqiao, the Buddha’s countenance blooms forever; the blood-calling cuckoo calls as the prayer beads hang askew. How many idle inscriptions lie by one's ear!
Verse: In vain, the spring breeze fails to reach my home. Walking by the stream, I sing while leaning on my purple wisteria staff.

Falling flowers bury my knees as I call out to the yellow orioles. The spring pond is moonless; I labor in vain, dredging its depths. I shall soon knock at the gates of the Lotus Land to inscribe my name there. Chorus (Zhuansha): The spring breeze does not reach my home. Singing as I walk by the stream, I lean upon my purple wisteria staff. With flowers falling ankle-deep, I cry out to the yellow orioles. The spring pond holds no moon; I dredge it all for naught.
I shall soon knock at the gates of the Lotus Land to inscribe my name.
Dedication for the Pure Land Verses by Fuyuan:
North, south, east, and west, I have sought what I know; Fearing the head while identifying with the form, all has become delusion.
Even if one were to directly awaken to the reality prior to sound, One still requires Amitābha to serve as the guiding teacher.
The Buddhas of the ten directions praise the Western Land; it is not for no reason that they extend their broad and long tongues.
I only fear that those of deluded Chan will become addicted to quiescent extinction, mistakenly taking annihilation for true permanence.
The Land of Tranquil Light is not different from the Land of Adornment; moving upward, one does not practice a dhyāna of annihilation. The subtle sounds of insects proclaim the Dharma-realm;
how could the Buddha-voice turn its back on that which has not yet arisen?
A Poem on Cherishing the Pure Land by Shen Langqian:
Do not doubt the Dharma of non-arising; Toil not in pushing back against the palm of Yanling. Gather your coins and hold your *nien-zi* beads;
When all six lines are auspicious, that is Amitābha.
Pure Land Verses by Ouyi:
The Western Land is precisely the land of one’s own mind; Maintain pure precepts firmly and do not let them slacken. All human realms are but cramped and confined environments;
There is no need to seek a peaceful dwelling in a foreign inn.

The Western Land is precisely the realm of Mind-only. One’s practice should accord with the teachings daily and remain fresh. If even for a single breath one does not persist, who can exert such effort?
How could one allow one's diligence to fall short of the former sages?
Pure Land Verse by Yongjue:
As soon as a single thought arises, one is immediately ensnared by entanglements. Nothing surpasses the mindfulness of the Buddha for gathering the mind. Directly cast the entire Sahā world aside;
the nurturing of the spirit truly rests upon the purple-gold lotus.

Hearing the Verses on the Recitation of the Buddha’s Name, one studies that the power of the vow is as heavy as a mountain, while rebirth [in the Pure Land] is as light as a feather. When seeing and knowing merge in a single thought-moment, this is the Sutra of the Names of Immeasurable Buddhas.

In these poems on contemplating the Pure Land, I see the lotus gradually appearing as my hair and beard grow streaked with frost. I examine my own failings and reflect upon them; what achievements have I actually accomplished in this single lifetime?
How many mornings and evenings remain of these hundred years? One must immediately resolve to seek the secure dwelling; do not continue to resign yourself to following the current.
The gate of death stands before you; the Land of Bliss is not far, and the path for returning exists. Go gladly to the Lotus Throne to behold the Compassionate Honored One.
I urge you to practice mindfulness of the Buddha:

sink into the pond of wisdom, recognize that this very day is the time, and only then will you know that yesterday was in vain. Cultivating practice is originally very easy; why did you not take refuge early?
The mind runs westward;
among those in the world who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, many see [the Buddha] but few actually behold Him. Many know that there is a Pure Land, yet few are born therein.
Why is this? It is because their minds are not single-minded. For the mind is the basis of the sixth consciousness; it should serve as the guide for the five sensory consciousnesses.
The master [of the mind] is instead enticed by the ears, eyes, mouth, and nose through their various cravings; thus, the mind becomes a slave to the five consciousnesses.

Once this servitude is fully established, even when the five consciousnesses have no sensory contact, they do not cease to enslave the mind. Consequently, it remains in a state of constant turmoil and agitation, finding no moment of peace.
This is why those who are entirely unaware of reciting the Buddha’s name naturally follow the six sense organs and undergo rebirth in the hells.

As for their retribution: those who know that there are both blessings and transgressions within the Buddha-dharma, even if they obtain a human body, will still return to this chaotic and impure world.
Only those whose minds exclusively course toward the West take the single-minded focus as their sovereign;
thus, they are able to manifest the fruit in the Western Land. The Sovereign is none other than the Tathāgata; one acts by making the mind the sovereign.
Taking the Buddha as one’s sovereign is what Mencius meant by "first establishing the great," so that the small cannot usurp it.

This corresponds to what the *Sūtra* says: "The very mind creates the Buddha; the very mind is the Buddha. Although this does not exhaust the full meaning of the correct interpretation, it may be understood through this secondary application.
Yunqi said: "One mind without distraction" means that the mind-king and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are all undivided. Now, regarding...

Although the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) are manifold, consisting of eight and fifty-one categories respectively, when one traces them back to their source, they do not transcend the single mind.
Now, for the practitioner of *nien-fo*: first, the ear-consciousness hears the name of that Buddha; next, the mental consciousness focuses its attention upon it with mindfulness.
Because of this focused mindfulness, the six sense faculties are collectively gathered, and the consciousnesses of the eyes, nose, tongue, and body all cease to function.

One practices. By not ceasing this mindfulness, when mindfulness reaches its limit, it becomes forgetfulness. That which is called "constant and thorough deliberation" (vitarka-vicāra) then becomes still.
By not ceasing this forgetfulness, when forgetfulness reaches its limit, it becomes transformation. That which is called the "conjunction of the real and the false" then has its falsity eliminated.

Consequently, the seventh consciousness and the eighth consciousness also cease to function. When the master no longer functions, how can the followers remain attached? This is the fifty-first [section].
What need is there for further discussion? At that moment, the great waves and ripples all became still water; the thick clouds and thin mists were entirely transformed into a clear sky.
Is this not the Western Land manifesting in the present?
With single-minded intent,
my thoughts race westward toward the Great Wisdom of the Fourth Buddha of Infinite Life,
whose wondrous marks number eighty-four thousand; can this not be the Amitābha of our own fundamental nature, dwelling afar across ten million billion lands?

This is precisely the Pure Land of Mind-only. Although purity and impurity are separated, how could they transcend one's own mind? Although the states of birth and Buddhahood differ, how could they deviate from one's own nature?
The essence of the mind is vast and empty, unimpeded by coming and going; its nature is fundamentally all-encompassing—how could it be hindered by grasping or rejecting?
Therefore, with a single thought, one ascends to the Treasure Realm and returns to one’s native home on the earth. In the snap of a finger, one gazes up upon the Compassionate Countenance;
truly, one reunites with the Father and Son of True Nature. For how many lifetimes have we been ungrateful for your virtue, needlessly enduring the depths of samsara?

Today, as we cast ourselves in sincere devotion, we shall surely receive your salvation. With the three minds fully awakened, our single resolve hastens toward the West; we shall rely upon you until the very end of time.
Praising you through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust;
cherishing An-yang as my native land, I have written this poem.

For several years at Chan-cha Hermitage, the sleeves of my robes have been stained with the dust of the capital. My aspirations soar above the clouds, yet I cannot stretch them forth. With the cry of a southern wild goose, a dream of home stirs.
Severed. Through the autumn wind, tears fall repeatedly all night long. If you do not now conceive a plan to return home, who will you rely upon hereafter to form a virtuous bond?
Look at the decayed bones buried by the roadside; most of those within are people who have never returned.
In years past, it was easy to part from the jade tower; originally, I had no intention of traveling far.

Who would have thought that now my hair hangs white as snow, while my solitary heart is ever suspended like the moon on the western hook? Suddenly, within my pillow, I hear the "bird longing for home"; outside the railing, I am frequently startled by the falling leaves of autumn.
With a single incense stick of sandalwood smoke and a single strike of the chime, I gaze idly into the distance as tears flow down my cheeks.
A Poem for the "Recalling the Buddha" Pavilion by Xue Xi:
There is an ancient saying: "In a hundred years of human life, those who reach seventy are rare. I shaved my head at sixty and was fortunate enough to join the ranks of the monastic community.
Now, having happily reached seventy, I am but a man of the morning and evening, with not long remaining in this world. It is not that I do not recite [the scriptures] in my daily life; yet—
While reciting the sutras, he still felt regret that his focus was not yet sufficient. He then took the passage from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* concerning Avalokiteśvara and Śrī-Ābhāsvara:
"If a person remembers the Buddha and recites the Buddha's name, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present or in the future.

He commanded Xiao Xuan to "remember the Buddha," hoping this might serve as an introduction for seeing the Buddha at the moment of death. Furthermore, he composed a mountain verse to be appended [to it].
To the left:

drifting with the waves and following the currents, it moves gracefully. Within the sound of a single snap of the fingers, seventy years have passed. Have you not known how to recollect the Buddha from of old?
As you age, you must apply yourself even more strenuously. Once the ground of the mind has been swept clean until it is empty, the flowers of the heart will bloom in brilliant splendor.
Radiant and clear, I have reached a definitive realization that this body is seen as such. Amidst the dust and the shedding of the cicada’s shell, I smile in conversation;

there is a vow to seek again the beauty of late-life scenery, for which I harbor only a sincere heart of mindfulness toward the Buddha. As several strands of incense burn out, the spring grove grows cold;
a single lamp accompanies me by the deep night window. Rain nourishes the fragrant *śāntika* vegetables in the broken fields, and the wind through the pines in the falling stream awakens the scent.
O Wondrous Voice! I regret not returning home and have resigned myself to abandonment. Now that I have returned, what use is there for the "Song of the Man from Yue"?
With three mats, I shall allow myself to live in poverty as I grow old; there is nothing like the sublime state of recollecting the Buddha’s true nature.

Knowing that all worldly affairs are like a discarded cooking pot, I shall wear this alone upon my girdle for the rest of my hundred-year life. Resting quietly among the crags upon a rush mat at night, I shall simply offer tea beneath the pines.
Bowl in hand, I close my door and do not forget; I constantly call the Buddha to mind. May he always follow me like a shadow follows the body. In the monasteries of my youth, I beheld the patriarchs;
it is as if remembering the Buddha in this present moment. Simply finding peace on a patch of ground with three rafters at the bottom of a valley, I hang not a single thread of silk within my breast.
On the secluded path, fallen flowers float upon the stream; through the small window, slanting rays of the setting sun descend.
Pine branches. In the silent realm of ultimate truth, who knows who can see it? Only the Buddha has often entered my dreams and thoughts.

Early on, I sought out the histories of Shi and Han to study the art of composition, and I presumed that throughout my life I had attained vast learning. Yet I have cast aside every moment as it flows away like water;
when I reflect upon myself, it is ultimately but a floating cloud. Amidst leisure, I alone recognize the stability of my hidden self; who else knows this memory of such a sublime place?
The Buddha is diligent; Cao Cao and Liu Bei have long since passed away—where are they now? Three feet of weeds cover but a desolate grave.
I wish to see the Buddha come in this very life; how could the Buddha be distant from me now?

If one can maintain a single thought without weariness, the eye of wisdom will open without needing three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. The purple swallow and yellow oriole chant the wondrous meaning; the clear stream and white stones reveal it.
Jewel Terrace. One must know the path for returning home as it manifests; who says there is no one to pull one back?
Fame and profit are enemies that saw through bone with a hair-thin rope; even Zhuangzi compared them to a snail. In this floating life, there is nothing quite like this place;
if you wish to remember the Buddha, you must know this is the foremost strategy. If mother and child can simply dwell together under one roof, what need is there to flee afar from the dust and wind?
Just as I am about to set out on my journey, I shall cease all inquiries from this moment forth; let me sit steadily upon my reed mat within my paper screen.

For many years I have wandered in exile, my hair now like white silk; remembering the Buddha, I cannot forget him throughout the twelve hours of the day. Alas! I lament for myself, a wayward wanderer;
how many times have the flowers fallen from the branches by the roadside?

In my self-pity, I recall the Buddha with deepening longing in my later years; save for the Buddha, none can express my heart. Who says that ten thousand pieces of gold make for a good life as a guest?
In the end, it is not equal to a single meal at home in a village.
Reciting Western Verse while Facing North:

The northern mountains already know that now is the past; what is there that is not? I close my wattle gate deeply as the sun sinks toward its setting glow. The tips of the bamboo sway lightly as the new moon rises;
The waist of the curtain half-rolls as the lingering clouds return home. The essence of mountain and forest fills my breast; The fragrance of cypress and pine smoke pervades all.
A commoner in plain clothes, I sit in constant meditation upon a single mat of rush. My small mind flies westward after the setting clouds.

Chanting the One Original of the West—do not seek it elsewhere, for the Western Land is not far away. Take the single phrase "Namu Amitābha" as your koan; if you can maintain this throughout your life, there shall be nothing else.
Reflect: "The Land of the Lotus Buddha is yours to roam.
This Western Buddha-land surpasses birth in the heavens; it surpasses the conditioned immortals of Penglai; it surpasses kings, lords, and wealthy households;
