and one must know that it also surpasses sitting in deluded dhyāna."
In the West lies the blissful celestial palace, where lifespan is immeasurable and merit inexhaustible. Sentient beings lacking faith slander it through their perversions;
those children of the Buddha who possess the necessary conditions share the same path.
The scenery of the Western Land surpasses Penglai. Consuming qi and feasting on rosy clouds only nurtures the womb of calamity. Do not study the methods of exiting the spirit for cultivation;
instead, directly cause the withered tree to burst forth in blossoms.
The wealth and nobility of the Western Land surpass those of kings and lords; its various adornments are complete in every detail.
If you simply prepare a sincere heart to seek that realm, the evil paths of saṃsāra will cease all at once.
In the Western Quarter, the eyes are filled with lotus flowers; adorned with a hundred jewels, their splendor is beyond praise.
All those who are most virtuous dwell together in one place, their number unknown, exceeding many times the sands of the Ganges.
The shortcut to the Western Land for seeking birth is easy; it depends solely upon one’s own single thought of sincerity.
By adding diligence to cultivate merit and wisdom, one shall attain a name inscribed upon the High Grade of the Golden Terrace.
The West is truly our own home; the single phrase of Amitābha leaves no room for error.
If you can believe with full conviction and practice with sincerity, even an iron tree will bloom.
In the West, they enjoy the excellence of noble households; within ponds of the seven treasures bloom flowers of four colors. Food and clothing appear spontaneously without being fashioned;
their radiant marks and signs are free from even the slightest flaw.
Within the Pure Land that I cherish, I pay homage morning and evening, striving with diligent effort. I frequently enter its golden ponds and lotus wombs in my dreams.
Even if I were to grind my bones and shatter my body for ten million kalpas, it would not be easy enough to repay the kindness of my compassionate parents.
Six times a day he knocks upon the gate to inquire after his golden father; this stray infant, adrift and lost, when will he return?
When the conversation reaches the point where saṃsāra is endless, they gaze at one another, unaware that tears have soaked their robes.
The elder brother calls and the younger responds as they recite the name of Amitābha; they vow to deliver their entire family from the river of craving.
If you can maintain this resolve at all times, it will truly leave even the Buddha with no recourse.
Long ago there was a man named Wu Zicai, who knocked upon a coffin day after day, calling out, "Come back!
Although his physical traces had not yet departed from the triple world, he had already sent his spirit to dwell within the womb of the white lotus.
Aboard this ship coming from the West, I recall my native land; Above the four-flower pond, the evening breeze is cool.
Adrift and unable to endure the urgency of my longing to return, A single light sail is hoisted against the setting sun.
In the practice of Buddha-recollection, one must expect to reach the ultimate end. When the end is reached, both the recollection and the mind are withdrawn together.
Then the wind and waves of the bitter sea of Saṃsāra are stilled, and one sails steadily upon the red-lotus boat to the Land of Bliss.
One must form the conditions for the Lotus Assembly; abandon all notions of self and other. At no time should one fail to regard this as a rare encounter;
with joy, ascend together upon the vessel of liberation.
Out of attachment and views, you gave rise to greed and anger, burying the sixteen-foot golden body.
Today, fortunately returning to the Pure Society, you should not continue as before to stir up dust and wind.
To plant the nine grades of lotuses of the Western Land throughout the entire three thousandfold world-system of this defiled realm—upon careful reflection, there is no other method;
it requires nothing more than a single firm thought.
No hanging of mugwort or tiger effigies to celebrate the Dragon Boat Festival; instead, we turn solely toward the ancient site of practice in the West.
With a single incense stick rising from the burner and a single strike of the chime, the fragrance of lotus blossoms drifts through the six gates.
I harbor thoughts of the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*).

While dreaming, I weep and pray toward the Buddha that death may come soon; then, upon passing away, I shall obtain a small lotus flower. May it open so that I forever transcend the cave of birth and death.
In my dream, I weep and pray toward the Elder Golden Immortal (*Suvarṇa-ṛṣi*): "Grant me the aid of your hidden influence to spur me on. Innumerable lotuses bloom in the pond.
There is indeed; one must surely cultivate a single thought as clear as a mirror to avoid the pitfall of mere idle longing.
Having heard that the matters of the Western Land are vividly present, this journey must rely upon auspicious conditions.
Once the mind is polished until it shines like a mirror, one need not fear that Amitābha will not appear before one.

For long I have gazed upon my body and mind as I watched the setting sun; where the sun sinks away, the fragrance of lotus blossoms lingers. Waterfowl and wind-tossed trees seem to understand my intent;
yet I remain filled with sorrow, for the dream of the human world has not yet been forgotten.
Of the thirty-six stratagems, flight is best; with ten thousand voices crying out, death shall be our appointed end. How much time remains in this fleeting world?
Once the evening incense has burned out, one remembers the Golden Pond.
Ascending straight to a high tower, I gaze toward my native land; where the golden sun sets, the evening clouds are azure. I know full well that my parents have long been filled with sorrow and pity;
my bowels are broken as this drifting duckweed remains in a distant place.
How can one escape the cycle of birth and death? If this mind remains unenlightened, all effort is in vain. Now, I shall no longer dream of saṃsāra;
I will simply traverse this single journey through the human realm.
The living must form karmic ties with the dead; the living must practice the Chan of the deceased. Do not string clay pellets together on a single thread;
otherwise, you will enter the Yellow Springs in a state of dark confusion.
Pure Land Verse:
The setting sun in the west disperses purple mists; When the mind-ground is clear and pure, the lotus flower appears. Lift your head and you are on the road home;
If you do not believe, doubt will keep you across the sea.

Longing for the Pure Land, I, Chu Shi, day and night yearns to return but has not yet returned. As a traveler at the ends of the earth, my soul soars in dreams; upon waking, from where does the cry of wild geese pass?

Gazing toward my homeland until my sight fails, letters from home have grown scarce. How many times have I opened the window to watch the setting moon? My entire life has been spent leaning against the railing.
The slanting rays of sunset; within the golden pond are lotus roots like boats. I imagine the blossoms spreading for dozens of paces around.

I have heard that white cranes are celestial birds; day after day they fly here to deliver auspicious tidings. I wish to send a letter to my virtuous friends; surely they would know the heart of my entire life.
I long think of the Land of Bliss where I shall ultimately return; how could I bear to remain far away, clinging to this lotus pedestal?
I have come to pay my respects. A hundred years truly pass in the blink of an eye; I only fear that my worldly attachments in this Sahā world are too deep.
Upon the lapis lazuli ground stand banners of purple gold; the emerald pavilions open with windows of white jade. My talent falls short of what these writings might suggest;
though my physical body has not yet arrived, my mind has already surrendered. How many peacocks are there capable of speech? As for the kalaviṅka bird, its eloquence is surely fixed.
How many pairs? In pure dreams, one longs for the direct path home; at the end of night, one can do nothing but listen to the rhythmic beating of the drums.

Of the hundred years of human life, seventy are rare. Looking back upon past events, they are all seen as mistaken. Every time I weep for those of my own stream who have departed, where have they gone?
Idle, I cast aside the Pure Land and no longer think of returning. Fragrant clouds form before the emerald steps; numinous birds perch upon coral trees.
Soaring within, one realizes the Dharma-body free from illness and affliction; how much more so when partaking in the joy of Chan, forever forgetting hunger!
Do not compare the prison of the womb to the Flower Pond; hasten toward that pond to claim a branch. Seated upon the Great Flower, you become a Buddha-child;
what need is there for a compassionate mother to bathe an infant? With the mouth feasting on the true delicacy of Dharma-joy, the mind attains the wondrous gates of illumination.
Dhāraṇī. On the day I returned from my meditative retreat before the Prajñā Terrace, it caused me to long remember the Master of Yanmen.
A verse on the Pure Land:
The Lotus Land of Mount Yan is the Medicine King’s wondrous medicine; now it is all bestowed upon this Sahā world. Yesterday morning, he personally entered the sick man’s room.
Mouth: How can one speak of its enjoyment as being like something else?
If you wish to become a person of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, it is like encountering a grave illness and only then taking good medicine;
because the contrivances of discursive thought cannot produce it, the lotus fragrance that accords with the essence shines radiantly.
With single-minded sincerity, the power of the thought is fully raised; like a dream, the entire body falls into the mud and water. Dragging away the thought, one hurriedly blinks the eyes;
peach blossoms laugh as they enter the Wuling Brook.
Where the red wheel sets is my home; I only fear that at the moment of action, a single thought might err. When the Guide has not yet arrived, forget both coming and going;
heaven and earth are but a black lotus flower.

Longing for the Pure Land, I have wandered through the dust and wind from south to north along the ancient creek. Turning my head toward the West, I enter that realm frequently in dreams. Whenever I recite the Buddha’s name, I follow the fragrant grasses across the ford;
my heart of returning always reaches the shores of the lotus flowers. How pitiful that the cries of the cuckoo are so piercing—a thousand times more so than the single call of Amitābha.
A close friend of the phrase. Not studying the way of Guishan’s “acting as another species,” I shall rather dwell in the Pure Land for now to serve as a commoner.
In this poem on the Pure Land, I recall the time before my parents were born; how many years have passed since that pain pierced my heart? My true face was recently struck by poison.
With my hands, I bury a heart full of warm blood for the sake of Qinglian.
A Poem on the Pure Land by Zhuan-yu:

"In poverty, one suffers much for the sake of children and grandchildren; with wealth, one again fears that descendants will be few. When a man of the Way has finished his meal, there is nothing left [to worry about]."
Looking westward, wisps of white clouds drift away.
In the Pure Land Poems by Huìfú:
Layer upon layer of pavilions at Píngǔ Island— How many have reached this place in their own leisurely way? A single bend of the clear river stirs feelings of parting.
Regulate yourself. If you have no mind, I shall also rest.
In this poem on the Pure Land, the fate of ten thousand kalpas of rising and sinking is lamentable;
the bones scattered across Mount Sumeru are as chaotic as hemp seeds. Only now do I awaken and feel shame.
Ashamed, with tearful eyes at dawn and dusk, I think only of home.

In the poetry of the Pure Land, Shen Lang invites the lotus flower not to wrap itself in the womb of the six dusts. Within the cage of sun and moon, one fashions for oneself; I am prepared to cast aside this heap of impoverished bones.
Son, this spring dream must be personally pushed aside.
To take a step, one must seek out the hundred-foot pole; a man of spirit must deliberately slay the Lord of Loulan. He casually tramples across the soil that strikes the heart;
he will not permit you to stand before the flowers on horseback and gaze.
Pure Land Verse by Ouyi:
The Western Land is precisely the land of the mind alone. If you do not recognize the West, how can you recognize the mind?
Why do you mistakenly hope for sudden and perfect understanding, Yet treat fallen leaves as if they were gold?

The Western Land is precisely the land of Mind-only. Firm faith in the West is itself the mind of faith. If, in every thought-moment, one opens the understanding of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, there is no need to depart from the teachings for them to be profound and mysterious on their own.
The West is precisely the land of Mind-Only; to attempt to negate the West is to contradict the underlying principle. A single speck of dust in Sukhāvatī is equal to the ocean of lands;
even with divine eyes, one could not know its limits.
The Western Quarter is precisely the land of Mind-only; only when the land is purified does one realize that the essence of mind is empty.
If all winds of objective phenomena still cling to lingering thoughts, how can you recklessly speak of east or west?
The Western Land is precisely the realm of Mind-only; in this age of semblance, it serves as a bridge across the ocean of Dharma.
If one can possess faith for even a single kṣaṇa, one will already perceive the fragrance of jewels and flowers within the precious lake.
To Layman Zhuang Yongjue:
The Buddha in the West has long beckoned you; if you are willing to believe, know that the path is not far. Look back at where this thought arises:
the Saha world of kalpas past is transcended in this very moment.
To the Venerable Shidali:
There is a road to the West that is not difficult to traverse. Direct your thoughts toward the West and do not yearn for the East. Constantly recite the Buddha’s name as a child remembers its mother;
why worry that mother and child shall not meet?

Hearing this verse on the recollection of the Buddha, one learns to open the pure realm of the Western Paradise. Unstained by worldly sentiments, there shall be no one to accompany you on the path ahead; you must travel alone.
I urge you to practice mindfulness of the Buddha at Shen Zhitang;

if the mind is single-pointed, it will not be disturbed. After a long time, success will naturally be achieved. It requires only that your practice be matured; why worry that the path will not be traversed?

If practice is interrupted, progress will be difficult; by constantly cultivating the Way, it will naturally be accomplished. One’s mindfulness must be earnest, and one’s vows must be sincere from the heart.
Regarding the recitation of the Name:
this arises from the state of single-mindedness without distraction (*ekacitta-avikṣepa*); it is no easy matter. You, Zisi, should contemplate and choose what is good.
"Adherence. Yanzi’s "earnestly wearing it upon his breast" and Shun’s "truly adhering to the Mean" both speak of adherence.
Only after not deviating for three months can one speak of "wearing it upon the breast"; only through "purity and singleness" can one speak of "truly adhering.
Thus, the names and designations for this adherence differ from those based on limited merit and conditions; this is because [the practitioner] is born in the Western [Pure Land].

This is a matter of the mind. As for the causes and conditions of merit and virtue, there are still those who practice them within the realm of phenomena; therefore, they remain vastly distant [from this]. Thus, the *Amitābha Sūtra* states:
"To mindfully recite the name of Amitābha Buddha with a sincere heart—even a single utterance—extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.
An ancient master remarked: "When the single mind is bright, the accumulated delusions are suddenly emptied; it is like a dark room that has stood for a thousand years."

"A single lamp illuminates all at once; this is the effect of upholding the principle. However, one must not say of oneself that because the rational nature (li-xing) is not yet clear, the ritualistic holding (shi-chi) is of no benefit.
Although it is ritualistic holding, that which holds is likewise the mind. As the *Great Power* chapter on Complete Penetration says:
'Without relying on expedient means, one spontaneously attains the opening of the mind. By proceeding with a single-minded focus, there will naturally come a day of awakening. Confucius..."

He said: "To study when one is weary; once one has attained knowledge, it is the same. Indeed, in both the cases of "delighting in life" and "delighting in learning," Confucius does not mention the word "knowledge.

When it comes to the person who studies through weariness (*kunxue*), the fact that he does not employ the character for "knowledge" allows us to know that what is unclear within his breast is precisely what is meant by "weariness.
Thus, "weariness" refers to a state during study where there is distraction and dullness, a condition of helplessness. It can be understood as such.

One may imagine seeing it; yet, when one comes to know it, it is identical to the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Long ago, during the time of the Buddha, an old man sought to leave the household life.
Śāriputra and the other great disciples were all unwilling to ordain him, saying that he lacked roots of goodness over many kalpas.
The Buddha said, "In immeasurable kalpas past, this person was a woodcutter. When a fierce tiger was pressing him to the limit, he [saw] a great..."
Terrified, he climbed a tree and cried out, "Namo Buddha. By virtue of this root of goodness, he encountered me and attained deliverance, realizing the fruit of Arhatship.

Now, even a single invocation of the Buddha’s name while the mind is distracted shall not be extinguished for eternal kalpas; how much more so for one who maintains the name with focused resolve—how could such a person fail to attain rebirth in the Pure Land?
Holding Fast to the Name, Chapter Five:

A Verse on Mindfulness of the Buddha Spoken to Bai Xiaoshan At the age of seventy-one, I no longer devote myself to chanting. Reading the scriptures strains my eyes, and performing meritorious deeds I fear the toil and bustle.
How can one cross over with the eye of the heart? With a single recitation of Amitābha. Walking, it is Amitābha; sitting, it is Amitābha.
Even if one is as busy as a speeding arrow, do not neglect Amitābha. The day is fading and the path is long; my life has already been wasted.
Morning and evening, with a pure mind, simply recite the name of Amitābha. The realized person will surely laugh at me for having "too much Amitābha.
But what of the realized? And what of the un-realized? I universally exhort all beings in the Dharma-realm to together recite the name of Amitābha.
Gazing north from Shanxi toward the Pure Land, the clouds obscure it in the distance.
A single hook of the new moon curves white in the sky; what strategy can I devise for my desire to be reborn there?
Amitābha’s single thought resonates through a thousand voices.
My refined literary skills have no place to be used; fame and profit are already as empty as a dream.
I play with a single string of prayer beads in my hand, hearing only the name of the Buddha as my heart rejoices with vigor.
Having thoroughly examined the sūtras and the Vinaya, I repeatedly urge you to keep Amitābha in mind: a single recitation can exhaust the karma of a thousand lifetimes;
how much more so when one recites and maintains it with diligent persistence.
The bustling affairs of the world are all but empty flowers; beyond these lectures, nothing else remains to hang upon my teeth.
A single string of prayer beads with newly replaced thread—Amitābha Buddha has become my kinsman-foe.
With chrysanthemum brains and ginger sprouts, one meal is more than enough; how could I dare to waste effort on anything else?
From now on, my ten fingers shall have no leisure, for I shall devote the rest of my life to counting the prayer beads.
I shall spend my life merely reciting and burning [incense]; night after night, until the first or second watch, I lament my solitary figure in this world of dust.
Before the wind and beneath the moon, I wander freely in walking meditation.
Sad to say, Shandao has already passed away; yet his transformation reaches both old and young, who all turn toward him in devotion. With one recitation of the Buddha’s name, offer a single coin;
with one recitation, one Buddha ascends into the void.
Pure Land Poems, Part One The West, the Land of Ultimate Bliss, is universally honored; I exhort all people to enter this gate. If you have a mouth, do not waste it on idle debate;
Simply hold the Buddha’s name to pass through morning and evening.
The Western Land’s vast vows are widely propagated; apply yourself diligently to the single phrase of Amitābha.
Let it be clear and distinct without interruption, calling out with every voice the master within.

Go straight to the West without lingering; you must take full charge yourself. If you can but single-mindedly and exclusively recite the Buddha’s name, your name shall be fragrant within the Land of Lotus Flowers.
The path to the Western Gate is most clearly defined; with one phrase of Amitābha, hasten swiftly on the journey.
Arrive early to sit upon the Vajra Terrace, where you shall realize non-arising under the same name and the same title.
The shortcut to the Western Land surpasses Zen meditation; with one phrase of Amitābha, spur yourself on swiftly. Ten million *buddhakṣetras* away, you arrive in the snap of a finger;
for others, it is only that they lack firmness of their own minds.
The Western Land is easy to reach, yet few know it; do not doubt the path of practice.
Once the Six-Character Sutra is mastered through pure cultivation, one shall pay homage to Amitābha upon the golden lotus throne.
The Ancient Chant for Mindfulness of the Buddha:
Amidst walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, do not let the single phrase "Amitābha" cease. You must believe that the cause is deep because the fruit is deep;

thus, it will come to pass that you are mindful even when not intentionally striving to be so. If you can ensure that every thought-moment is not empty, you will surely achieve a state of unified mindfulness. While mindful, recognize this.
Contemplating others: Amitābha appears together with me.
From the *Pure Land Poems*:
"A string of prayer beads, dark and lustrous, atop a single peak; the circular reflections of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. Revolving in pure mindfulness, they are ever present."
Succession: letting go and picking up are both the same.
This manifest case is beyond deliberation. The dawn bells strike repeatedly as the wax candles burn long; throughout the six periods of day and night, the sound never ceases.
The fragrance of white lotuses wafts through the entire gate.
With Buddha in mind, one contemplates with the heart; when contemplation reaches the emptiness of the heart, even Buddha is forgotten. Casting off all attachments, one returns to examine once more:
blossoms bloom in red and white, interspersed with green and yellow.
Single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name; do not let the time slip away. How lamentable that the paths of human life are so many! Hasten to invoke the name of Amitābha Buddha;
do not drown your precious years in the river of craving.
A single phrase of Amitābha is superior to seated meditation; one sound not yet finished, another follows.
When the practice reaches its peak through every thought and every moment, everywhere is the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
A Verse on Mindfulness of the Buddha:
Utpalavarnā taught me to be mindful of Amitābha; How could I ever be separated from him? I do not know him, yet he is I;
Meeting face-to-face, we laugh heartily.
The single phrase of Amitābha is easy to recite; remember it morning and evening, never letting it depart.
As you recite and recite, the flower of the mind blooms—this is truly the time when Amitābha appears in the world.
Do you see the Amitābha of intrinsic nature? When asked what his countenance is like, they only know how to open their mouths and chant aimlessly.
Who knows that they have missed the mark at the very moment of speaking?
Within one's own home is a single Amitābha Buddha; without relying on cultivation, he is already manifest and complete. Do not say that he is entirely unseen before your eyes;
at a single call, there is a single response.
I contemplate Amitābha without a moment’s separation; one "Amita" finished, then another "Amita. Amitābha calls out to Amitābha and asks:
"You are Amitābha; who am I?"
I contemplate that Amitābha does not reside in sound; the lofty mountains and flowing waters are his true intimates.
On a night deepened by stillness under the bright moon, the broad tongue proclaims the fragrance of white lotuses.
With every sound one recites the Buddha’s name, how long is the intention! It is just like a doting child calling for its mother.
When one reaches the point where a single sound resonates in response, the true parents and child rejoice beyond measure.
I gladly send these golden characters upon the golden lotus; with one phrase of Amitābha, I vigorously spur myself on.
Casting aside all worldly belongings from the very start, I shall take a seat within the flowery carriage.
Repentance purifies the Pure Land;
though the distance be but a few feet, the golden countenance and white hair-brow appear. Is it in vain to single-mindedly recite the Name? At dawn, ten thousand recitations ascend upon the sun;
at night, a thousand invocations rise with the moon. Through years of shifting heat and cold, one never tires; thus the natural mother and child meet.
Having met [the Buddha], how can one describe the sufferings of Sahā? These painful matters are as numerous as the bristles on a hedgehog.
Sitting alone in leisure, facing the West, I hold the prayer beads in my hand, reciting without forgetfulness. The name of the Buddha can purify the ground of the mind;
the tongue-root then becomes fragrant like the scent of lotus roots. As the radiant sun reaches the mountain’s edge, shimmering gold floats everywhere.
The light of the chamber. In this realm and at this time, there is no separate perception; you are permitted to witness King Drumasvara directly.
On the eve of the year’s end, ascending the hall, he produced three rhymes on "Much Sa-po" (Sahā) and a six-character *Lotus Sūtra* that subsumes many meanings.
This single dharani is like chanting "Sa. Since following the direct path toward the West.
Go! You have idled away the Way-showering Old Lady of Mount Tiantai.

She showed me that there must be death following birth; what need is there to debate long or short? Now that I have attained the marks of a fully ordained monk, the vows of my entire life are fulfilled.
You should give rise to great joy; by no means harbor grief or distress. Let go of all external conditions and with single-mindedness recite the Buddha’s name.

Focus your thoughts on the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where you shall be born upon a lotus of the highest grade. There you will see the Buddha and awaken to non-arising, returning once more to deliver all beings.
In response to Empress Dowager Cisheng’s inquiry regarding those who possess the honor, dignity, and nobility of high status:
it is because they have planted roots of goodness in past lives. Since the causes are superior, the fruits will surely flourish; thus, they now constitute a great mass of merit.
Profoundly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit, one plants further causes within the fruits [of past deeds]. This is like flowers upon brocade; their layered beauty is inexhaustible.
Having thus cultivated merit, one should furthermore observe with caution: to cultivate merit without cultivating wisdom is ultimately not the cause of liberation.
Cultivate both merit and wisdom; they are supreme, both mundane and supramundane. The true nature of wisdom within sentient beings is obscured by discursive thoughts.
The essential gateway for cultivating wisdom is simply to mindfully recite the Buddha’s name. When mindfulness reaches its peak, the mind becomes pure; when the mind is pure, the land is also pure.
Born within the most supreme lotus throne, one beholds the Buddha and awakens to non-arising;
ultimately attaining the path of Buddhahood, peerless throughout the three realms—this is called the Great Noble One.
A Pure Land Poem by Xueqiao:
One, two, three, four, five, six, seven— With single-mindedness and no distraction, one is reborn in the West.
Though the Buddha’s words seem easy to recite, The moment you take a step, your whole body sinks into the mire.
A Poem on the Pure Land, Author Unknown:

Bind your mind to a single phrase: Amitābha. Whether in daily life one is at leisure or busy, whether few or many [recitations], If one does not attain wondrous awakening by the end of life, It will still allow one to depart from Saṃsāra with one's karma remaining.
Verse for Recollecting the Buddha:
With eyes fixed on the thoughtless recollection of the Ancient Amitābha, When one reaches the state of no-mind, one’s lifespan increases. The Sovereign King Acala manifests his entire body;
At every step, golden waves surge from beneath one’s feet.

When mindfulness is free from the thought of mindfulness, it is forever unobstructed. When mindfulness reaches the state of no-mind, one has truly left the household life. Moving spontaneously and freely, following wherever the feet turn;
with every step of coming and going, one treads upon lotus flowers.

With a pure mind toward the Land of Bliss, Shenlangqian has spent forty-nine years paying off the debts of his lips and mouth. These seventeen hundred cases of entangling vines—the old monk, fearing worldly affairs, has cast them all aside;
he idly passes his time in reciting "Namo."
Fiercely grasping the butcher’s blade, he cuts through the nest of craving; in his hand, he masters both life and death, refusing to spare a single soul.
The six characters of his great name leave a trail of blood with every stroke of the blade—this is no mere matter of the wind blowing past a donkey's ears.
Haphazardly donning the *kāṣāya*, he leads the way; holding the name is not a matter of following one's whims.
With a single sound he goes straight ahead, leaving no trace—most like a gray falcon just released from its leather tether.

Chanting the Nien-fo verse ten thousand times takes the Buddha-sun as its compass; upon hearing the cock crow, one should rise and maintain the practice. A bridge to the Land of Ultimate Bliss extends from the pillow;
this very body has already sat within the azure lotus pond.
The Verse on Holding the Name with Single-mindedness and Without Distraction:
The mind’s dullness and distraction are like clouds and mist; Ten thousand kalpas of teachings are shattered this very day. The great earth and the cosmos pass through a single phrase;
Every sound cuts off the paths of a thousand divergences.
Since settling my mind at midnight, I have not had further doubt from that point on. With both eyes wide open, heaven and earth are vast;
in this era of Great Peace, there are no signs, even unto this day.
Pure Land Verses by Ouyi:
The Western Land is precisely the land of one’s own mind; A single string of bright pearls, the myriad practices perfected. When the beads snap, the thread must be changed again and again;
The ticket to the Lotus Land leaves no room for further fault.
Having already placed faith in the boat of Amitābha’s great vows through the verses of the Buddha-assembly, we shall together cultivate samādhi to cross the stream of delusion.

Practicing the Way during the six periods of the day without other thoughts, let the single great name be as urgent as saving one's head from fire. One should feel deep pain for the blind turtle that remains forever submerged; may you alone rejoice in the hole of the floating wood.
Now drifting, he earnestly presses into the principle of non-arising; by the edge of the Seven Treasures Pond, they stroll hand-in-hand.
At the Shilin Pao-an hermitage, the Buddha-name of Yongjue resonates in a continuous stream.
It is just like smelting true gold with a fierce fire: when the ore is exhausted, the gold remains whole and becomes great.
Functioning as a mirror that reflects the earth and illuminates the heavens, its discernment is clear and distinct;
the Buddha’s name is as direct as a sword leaning against the sky, severing thousands and tens of thousands of branches.
Before one’s very eyes lies the Land of Lotus Flowers—what need is there to concern oneself with the compassionate power of Amitābha’s vows?
In the Verse on Mindfulness of the Buddha:
"With a single phrase of Amitābha, there is no other thought; when myriad thoughts are all empty, the primordial nature is revealed. This is liberation in every dust mote;
there is no need to further inquire of the Patriarchs' Chan."
I show my friend Wu that the single gate of nianfo (Buddha-recitation) is the most direct and straightforward. It requires no extensive knowledge or understanding; it employs no clever speech.
It demands only this one phrase: "Buddha. Resolute as a piece of steel, it takes no account of kindness or affection, nor does it concern itself with resentment or enmity. All other thoughts—
Neither arises; the shadow of the Sahā world vanishes of itself.
Hearing the verse on mindfulness of the Buddha, the student and mother shall not be parted.
Pure mindfulness shall always succeed one another. How excellent is Mahāsthāmaprāpta, who has attained this inexhaustible intent!

**Verses on Cherishing the Pure Land** By Lien Yin A single phrase of Amitābha is a lotus blooming amidst the flames; The five types of teachings cannot fully describe it. If every sound is uninterrupted, demonic obstacles will stay afar;

If every thought is without error, the Buddha appears before one. After many kalpas of delusion, the roots of affliction are utterly uprooted; Through a lifetime of diligent effort, the fruit is realized.
It is capable of fulfillment. Sentient beings, possessing consciousness, share the same essence. If one simply resolves their will, who could not achieve it?
Ordinary people are weak and inferior; visualization is difficult for them to accomplish. By simply practicing the recitation of the Name, one will attain rebirth.

If, until the very end, the mind remains undiverted, the Buddha himself will come to welcome one at the moment of death. Worldly conditions are easily defiled, like honey on a blade; the aspiration for the Way is difficult to maintain, like water [on a lotus leaf].
Floating on the surface of the water, the scenery of this land of bliss is truly not bad. Return home early; compose your verse for the journey through the night.
I urge you to practice nianfo at Shen Zitang:
human life is entirely illusory, and all things are ultimately empty. If you wish to reach the Western Heaven, it depends entirely upon these six characters.
Do not say that the years are good; time passes with rapidity. To recognize the path of skillful means, there is only the recitation of Amitābha’s name.

When the sacred realm manifests before one, it is as if all Buddhas and Tathāgatas enter the minds and thoughts of all sentient beings, like the rising sun appearing in the heavens, its reflection manifesting in a hundred ways.
It is like a river. Even if the sun is in the sky, if the water in the river is turbid, one cannot see it;

therefore, one must employ the gate of contemplation through *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) to clear the turbid waters and develop the eye of the mind, thereby broadly perceiving the impermanence of the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment). A sutra states:

"When a person is about to die, their body and mind are in agony; one should cause the dying person to contemplate the Buddha’s *lakṣaṇa* and *anuvyañjana* (physical marks and minor characteristics), moment by moment..."

[He] caused [them] to continue and to give rise to the bodhicitta. Furthermore, he extensively explained for them that the three realms are difficult to dwell in and that the three miserable destinies are fraught with suffering;
he taught that only the Buddha’s bodhi is the true refuge. Alas! This is the Tathāgata’s compassionate pity for sentient beings, his heart of striving to rescue them at the moment of death.
The Buddha said: "The mind at the point of death possesses immense power; therefore, at the time of death..."

The thought at the moment of death can dissolve even heavy karma. Nevertheless, I have observed that among those who have practiced *nien-fo* throughout their lives, there may still be some whose bodies are oppressed by pain at the time of their passing, or whose tongue becomes short and stiff, rendering them unable to recite the Buddha’s name.

How much more so for those who have not mastered the practice of visualization during their daily lives; when they are tormented by the eight sufferings and pressed from all sides like four mountains closing in, how could they possibly maintain awareness?
Recite the Buddha’s name with the mouth of consciousness, each sound uninterrupted; practice contemplation so that the mind does not become distracted.
This must surely be because the roots of goodness from past lives are profound and far-reaching; how could such a thing be expected of ordinary, indolent sentient beings?

It must be as stated in the *Contemplation Sūtra*: "Except for the time one sleeps, one should constantly keep this matter in mind," and it further says, "Whether emerging from or entering meditative concentration, one constantly hears [the Buddha]."
The Sublime Dharma is precisely where one finds secure footing.
When the sacred realm manifests before one, this is the sixth pure land. [Verse by] Āśvaghosa.
Spontaneous music provides boundless delight; seven-jeweled towers and terraces rival the beauty of the sun and dawn.
Exquisite fragrances never dissipate, as celestial flowers rain down from amidst the clouds in profusion.
The Verses on the Nine Grades of Lotus Flowers by Lü Chūnyáng:
Emerging resolutely from the golden pond, Each petal holds jade dew. It releases wondrous fragrance amidst the flames; Its color is as firm as bodhi.
The mind is the image of the terrace; the lotus, by virtue of its color, is the body. There is no specific location in the West; in Ultimate Bliss, one awakens to the empty and true.
Within the twin rows of trees is a lump of mud; amidst the nine grades of lotuses is nectar. The kalaviṅka bird does not understand non-arising, yet it flies toward the depths of the Ganges.
Last night, the celestial wind blew upon the Northern Dipper; the black dragon and the lion roared together. If you wish to see the lotus, where shall you seek it?
The lotus is right within the Tathāgata’s mouth.
Enlightenment has no tree, and the mirror has no stand; how could the nine grades of lotuses bloom? Entrust this to Tongyuan and cease your vain awakenings;
the two characters "guest-dust" (adventitious defilements) certify one as a Tathāgata.
The Way-man is accustomed to being loquacious; he wishes to discourse upon the colors of the lotus. It does not grow within the four assemblies of this Sahā world;
it is unstained by blue, yellow, red, white, or black. From time to time he enters contemplation and beholds the Tathāgata; the willow flowers sway like the moon of his jeweled necklaces.
Verse for Rebirth:
May Avalokiteśvara come from afar to welcome me, And Śākyamitra assist from the distance to greet me. The precious vase shines upon my crown; The transformation Buddha appears clearly before my head.

Together we shall travel through the lands of the ten directions, holding flowers and awaiting the ninth birth. I pray that with your hands of compassion, you will uplift and guide me as we journey together toward the West.
In the Pure Land, I sing of Li Qinglian [Li Bai] facing the setting sun;
from afar I gaze upon the face of Great Compassion: eyes as pure as the waters of the four seas, and a body radiant as a mountain of purple gold.

Through diligent mindfulness, one will surely attain rebirth; therefore, it is called "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī). With nets of pearls, trees of precious jewels, celestial flowers scattered about, and fragrant pavilions—these images appear as if before my very eyes.
I vow to entrust myself to that sacred site (bodhimaṇḍa). By means of this ocean of merit, may there be secret protection to serve as a bridge for my passage.
The sins of eighty billion kalpas will be swept away like light frost by the wind. May I behold Amitāyus and forever gaze upon the light of his white tuft.
At the moment of death, may I be reborn in the West;

throughout my life, may I recite the name of Amitābha and contemplate his white tuft in every thought. By maintaining this non-retrogressive mind, I shall certainly be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.
In the western retreat, amidst the vines, the Moon Lord says:
"The Land of Bliss is my home. I smile at myself as a drifting guest on a distant road. A single point of returning heart hangs upon the setting sun;
A hundred years of illusory affairs are lodged in empty flowers. The navel-wheel does not stir as the sutra-curtains roll up; The olfactory perception remains ever pure as the incense burns.
The threads slant; right mindfulness forms a state free from external things. Through the small window, the trees lining the path form a lush, intermingled green.

Thinking of the West—pointing westward from the mountains of Beishan, further west beyond Jambudvīpa, and continuing westward toward the *caitya* (temple)—the lotuses bloom in full splendor, their light without peer.

At night, the ground is spread with lustrous lapis lazuli, utterly free of mud; the wind stirs the sounds of the Dharma like the eightfold chanting. The pools flow with waters of virtue, surpassing the Double River.
At the end of life, one need only attain rebirth beyond this world; let the nine grades follow their respective levels, low by low.
From here to the west, across ten trillion worlds—where mountains stretch long and waters flow far—who can know the way? Only through the gate of contemplation is the path home direct;
sitting in stillness, the kalpa-water becomes as clear and azure as lapis lazuli.
Sitting upright, I first cultivated the contemplation of water; A slight breeze did not stir, and the emerald waves were level. Who can see this profound and secluded realm?
A single expanse of lapis lazuli shines brightly before the eyes.
Out of weariness with this Sahā world, they seek a pure land; their thoughts and imaginings race toward it from dawn until dusk.
Who would believe that without moving a single step, one may find towers and pavilions deep within the clouds?
Who would have known that sitting upright, one can yet travel? In an instant, the mind soars to the Jade Tower. The shadows of bamboos and the moonlight shift across the windows and doors;
one further suspects the walking trees are now upon the eaves.
The nine grades of lotus flowers are arranged in succession; surely their emerald leaves must press against one another. I know not on what day I shall be born into the Lotus Realm;
alas, morning and evening weigh heavily upon my heart.
Verse One: Western Pure Land How wondrous is the fruit of the Western Pure Land! The *utpala* lotuses bloom throughout the realm. Various manifestations truly constitute great prosperity:
Upon each single flower pedestal sits a Tathāgata.

The Western Land is not far; it lies upon the immediate path. To directly accept and take responsibility for it in a single instant—whatever meets the eye and whatever encounters the conditions—all is Sukhāvatī.
As the waters flow and the wind moves, they proclaim the Mahāyāna.
The great earth of the western quarter is of golden hue; jeweled trees reaching to the heavens proclaim the sounds of the Dharma.
Such is the name of the Land of Peace and Bliss, where the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties can never again invade.
Within the Pure Land, the peaks of Mount Sumeru once bore the light of the Sun and Moon; he was instructed to maintain mindfulness of the West.
Since personally realizing samādhi, he has never been apart from the side of the Compassionate Honored One.
This single scroll of the *Amitābha Sūtra* is my letter from home. In the direction where the sun sets, there is my old dwelling.
Prepare ample provisions and expect to arrive early, lest it cause my compassionate father to sigh in lamentation day after day.
When turbid water is completely cleared, the pearl has its power; when the distracted mind does not move, the Buddha has no occasion to act. Before one’s eyes, everything is the path home;
there is no need to seek a guide from others.
Within the Great Perfect Mirror, all dust and defilement are severed; amidst the azure lotus flowers lies the sacred embryo.
Gazing afar beyond the pools of golden sand, the precious light constantly illuminates the jade towers and terraces.
Praise of the Pure Land:
The world of Sukhāvatī is made of pure lapis lazuli. Rows of jewel-trees stand in order throughout the four quarters. Gold sand is spread upon the ground, and silver stairways form the paths.
Jade and gemstone balustrades encircle it in seven tiers.
Regarding the *Pure Land Poems*, the poem by the Confucian scholar Chushi says: "In hewing the handle of the axe, the pattern is not far off. The commentators say:
"If one holds the handle of the axe to hew another handle and looks askance at it, one still considers it far. Believing these words, our school’s practice of nianfo (Buddha-recitation) is solely...
From my own mind, with the desire to see the Buddha, the Buddha manifests from the mind. Amitābha Buddha’s thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs are inherently complete by nature;
they do not require seeking from without. His supernormal powers and radiance extend to the furthest limits of the future, and thus he is named Immeasurable Life (Amitāyus).
As for the lotus ponds, jeweled thrones, crystal palaces, and jade towers—each and every pure realm is likewise so.
All of these arise from the wondrous joy of one’s own mind. It is said: "If one perceives the Amitābha of self-nature, one immediately realizes that the Pure Land is but the mind alone.
This is as the Buddha commanded Ānanda during the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi* assembly:

"All phenomena of floating dust and various illusory transformations are produced where they are and perish where they are; through the conjunction of causes and conditions, there is a false arising."
The separation of causes and conditions is called "extinction" in name only, for it is a false construct.

One fails to realize that arising and ceasing, going and coming, fundamentally exist within the Tathāgatagarbha—the eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, and truly constant nature. Within this, one seeks going and coming, delusion and awakening, or birth and death, yet finds nothing at all.
Since nothing is found, there is but the One Mind. If the Pure Land arises through conditions and the defiled land ceases through conditions, then...

The seal of the Sahā world perishes; this perishing is also an illusion. If the practices of the defiled land cease and the practices of the pure land flourish, then the manifestation of Sukhāvatī is accomplished;
this accomplishment is also an illusion. Yet these cycles of arising and ceasing, of purity and defilement, do not depart from one’s own mind.

The mind does not perceive the mind, for no characteristic can be grasped. Though one is constantly engaged in grasping and rejecting throughout the day, there has never been any grasping or rejecting; though one is constantly engaged in thought and recollection, [there is nothing to be found].
One has never entertained such thoughts; thus, being there does not hinder the realization of the illusory, and being here does not hinder the cultivation of the illusory.

At the very moment of generating the bodhicitta, one has already attained perfect enlightenment. What obstacle could there be to the illusory elimination of habitual tendencies? One sits at the site of enlightenment as an illusion, and transforms sentient beings as an illusion.
If one has reached the ultimate fruit of illusion, how could one fail to understand the illusory phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane worlds, as well as the deeds of the Great Charioteer?
Formerly, Chan Master Tianyi Huai personally met Mingjue and exhausted the wondrous secrets not transmitted by the Buddhas and patriarchs.
He once practiced the Pure Land method. On the verge of his passing, he asked his students:

"If one says that one abandons the defiled to take up the pure, loathing this and rejoicing in that, this is the sentiment of grasping and rejecting—a deluded thought of sentient beings. Yet, if one says there is no Pure Land, that would contradict the words of the Buddha."
Regarding those who cultivate the Pure Land, how should they practice? He answered himself: "To be born is indeed to be born;
to go is truly not to go. No words surpass these. Those with resolve should all recite the Buddha's name.
As previously stated, the Pure Land of Mind-Only and the Amitābha of Self-Nature do not lie beyond one’s own door; how could they be far away?
One must contemplate the compassionate countenance of Amitāyus; it resides solely within the present moment of thought.
It cuts off the paths of coming and going between birth and death, encompassing earth, water, fire, wind, and space. Upon its crown is the *uṣṇīṣa* from which a thousand rays of light radiate;
its seat presses upon a cluster of brocade lotuses. Everywhere he ascends to precious pavilions, where pearls shimmer and jade is translucent.
When body and mind are set down, the Buddha appears before one; Ordinarily, the sounds of the Dharma fill the ears.

The wind and branches play only the melody of non-arising; The sun-gazing opens wide the dayless sky. Walking, one follows the clouds rising over the jade steps; Sitting, one leans against the moon’s beauty beneath the pearl trees.
When ordinary beings reach this state, they all become sages; Without passing through kalpas, the great fruit is perfected.
Not yet returned to Ultimate Bliss, I still dwell in Jambudvīpa; drifting through the dust and wind, how many autumns more?

Frequent nightmares are startled by the rain upon banana leaves; my native land lies only within the Lotus Continent. In the space of stretching and bending one’s arms, there is not much distance; I occupy the highest place among the multitude.
The two Great Beings, pitying me for my old age and illness, would it not be fitting to take my hand and enter the jade tower?
The Dharma King governs from his precious lotus palace; Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas fill the land within. His universal canopy is like the heavens above;
his great brilliance surpasses the sun rising in the east. His azure spiral topknot reaches the floating clouds; his white jade brow-hair outshines the rainbows spanning the sea.
To this peerless being of both the mundane and supramundane worlds, one should know that his essential nature is originally empty.
Devas and humans alike all realize spiritual powers; each possesses the same golden-hued marks.

They perform Buddha-works by scattering myriad exquisite flowers, while fragrant winds arise throughout worlds as numerous as dust motes and sands. When their bodies are touched by the light of his form, they become supple and soft.
Musical sounds from instruments proclaim suffering and emptiness. Leaning against carved railings, they gaze upon jeweled trees, within which lie boundless Buddha-lands.
How many times have I dreamed of the Dharma King’s palace? Coming and going with clarity, the path is unmistakable. Jewel banners rising from the water are like the sun and moon;
Precious canopies arrayed in the void resemble clouds and mists. Mandarin ducks bathe together in the waters of the golden pond;

Mynah birds pair off, each holding a flower from the jade tree. Sleeping so soundly, I do not know who has awakened me; A single burner of incense disperses its fragrance as the evening sun slants low.
One may sit upon the highest tier of the lotus throne; I grant that the power of an ordinary person’s vow can achieve this. In an instant, the human mind is transformed into Buddhahood;
in a mere moment, the visualization of water is changed into ice. Jade sprouts grow from the agate trees before the steps; golden cords encircle the lapis lazuli ground.
Infinite celestial flowers fill the lapels of one’s robes; one may soar at will through the Buddha-lands of the ten directions.
My robes do not harm silkworms, and my food does not require plowing. By the waters and beneath the trees, I delight in walking meditation; body and mind are joyful, free from all suffering.

The adornments of the primary and secondary bodies are perfected in a single lifetime. From moment to moment, Buddha-light radiates from my mouth; at every hour, celestial music resounds throughout the void.
Yet I find it regrettable that my shoes and socks are stained with mud; now, thousand-petaled lotuses are held up before my feet.
Seeking the Land of Ultimate Bliss to the West through many words, one ultimately does not depart from the pure mind. Empty reflections entering the pond are all emerald;
sunlight piercing the trees is entirely gold. Though these phenomena are like dreams and illusions and are not real, when the principle is reached, it is perfectly eternal and profoundly deep.
Regarding the eighty-four thousand marks and signs of true form, I entreat you to sit upright and strike upon the spiritual breast.
My home lies in the Jade Capital at the western extremity; in my old age, it is hard to dispel the longing for my native land.

Whenever I gaze upon the crescent moon first appearing above the clouds, I first think of you, the foremost among the blossoms. Dense and sparse are the shadows of the jade trees; coming and going are the cries of waterfowl.
The red pavilions and purple halls are ever beautiful in spring; even with brush and ink, no artist could paint them.
I myself practice mindfulness of the Buddha and cultivate dhyāna. I rejoice that my square robe and crown-marks are complete.

Having cultivated the fruits of merit through many lifetimes, I have now established the karmic conditions of incense according to the nine grades. My name, [insert name], is inscribed within the deep petals of the flower; in a dream, I am beside the long star and the setting moon.
The defiled ordinary person and the pure Buddha—these two pearls, black and white, are threaded together upon a single strand.
Boundless Great Beings and Śrāvakas—how could this vast assembly not be divided chapter by chapter? The sages of this single assembly remain eternally in samādhi;

those coming and going from the ten directions all travel upon clouds. They discuss the profound mystery beneath the *maṇi* water of the trees; they recite the Buddha’s name amidst the flocks of *jīvañjīvaka* birds in the groves.
Whether sitting, reclining, or walking, they encounter no obstruction; celestial flowers fall in profusion everywhere.
Gazing westward, I behold the crimson clouds and the white solar disc; looking upward, I behold the precious throne and the body of purple-gold. One realm is pure, and every realm is pure;

when the thought arises, the mind is true, and in every moment, it is true. Born into the city of Ultimate Bliss, one shall never again fall back; throughout the entirety of empty space, there is not a speck of dust.
Having previously drifted and submerged in the sea of suffering, how fortunate I am now to be one who has reached the other shore!
Pure Land Poem:

Ancient Beyond that stream, there are no evil realms, and their very names are unheard of. All the myriad sounds become the voice of *nien-fo*. Fine rills flow through the channels like the tuning of a brocade zither;
a gentle breeze blows through the trees, playing a jade flute. Cranes descend before the emerald curtains; the people dwell upon crystal ground.
Ascending upward, the practitioner proceeds with a serene and undisturbed mind; resplendent celestial music spontaneously comes to welcome them.
Ten thousand *yojanas* of the long journey fit upon the tip of a single hair—how can it be said that the path to the West is vast and boundless? The Buddha-realm is not to be seen outside the mind;
the true countenance is mostly beheld within meditative concentration. A parrot nests amidst clusters of precious flowers; it perches upon the branches of the jade tree.
Phoenix and Peacock. The ancient family of Qingtai welcomes the assembly from the sea; when wind and clouds meet, there is a cry of joy.
A Verse on the Pure Land by Boshan: "The pure mind is itself the land of the West;
when the brocade of the universe is complete, the karma of purity is fulfilled. As soon as the single phrase of Amitābha is uttered..."
Emerging, the dignified leather bag is vast and empty;
the pure mind is itself the Western Land. A single phrase of Amitābha is a Buddha’s fulfillment; the entire great earth becomes a world of silver.
Where else could one behold the morning star?
A pure mind is the Western Land; words have no substance, for walking there is most intimate.
Lightly striking the worn wooden fish, how many rains of flowers fall in chaotic profusion!
In the Pure Land, the poem says:
Lanqian and Chenzhen hang nets from the incense altar; Kaling’s smooth voice calls out several times.
Amidst the groves, they joyfully meet their golden companions, Together carrying flower-baskets to await the Tathāgata.
Verses on the Subtlety of the Sun-Viewing Platform:
A single bright mirror has been sealed by kalpas of dust; The path to Amitābha lies but a few feet away, yet remains impassable. All phenomena are but mind—this was first illustrated through the sun;
Thus we know the Great Awakened One is none other than the Mind-Elder.
Chanting on water, one observes ice forming as lapis lazuli;
suddenly it becomes water again, and suddenly it becomes ice once more. As the ice forms lapis lazuli, a precious pond is created. This wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and abides nowhere.
The marks arise according to the channels established from one's own mind.

The light of the jeweled banner consists of seven-jeweled golden banners formed of a hundred treasures. The eight-sided jewel beads uphold precious radiance; each ray of light contains eighty-four thousand [sub-rays].
The colors are such that the brilliance of a billion suns shines forth, illuminating the eyes with clarity.
From the edge of the Dharma-lotus banner-pedestal, musical instruments abound; the eight kinds of pure winds arise spontaneously, their melodic sounds carried by the wind through the void.
He sat cross-legged upon lapis lazuli, leaning his ear to listen.

He chanted the Contemplation of the Water of the Eight Virtues Pond (The Eight Virtues Pond is composed entirely of pearls and jade; that which forms the pond water is the treasure, and that which forms the treasure is the pearl. Lotus flowers grow within the pond, and as the water flows between the flowers, it proclaims the sublime Dharma).

The Dharma is also produced by this jewel. That the golden light transforms into a precious bird to praise and extol the Triple Gem, and that the golden light surges forth, is likewise produced by this jewel.
The pond opens with precious lotuses;
the pearls form the seven treasures, and the treasures form the pond. The pond is fashioned with fourteen branches of golden channels. The lotus flowers are not merely as large as chariot wheels.
Behold the Buddha’s attainment of Buddhahood—such-and-such a person was present there.

The flowing water preaches the Dharma as droplets of pearl-water meander around the sublime lotus. Circulating upward and downward, the wheel of the Dharma is complete; the sounds of suffering, emptiness, and non-self emerge from every voice.
Furthermore, it transcribes the chapters on the Tathāgata’s marks and signs of excellence.

The birds' songs preach the Dharma, and the light of the jewels transforms them into birds; their harmonious warbling is the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. Within the waters of merit lies an inexhaustible treasury;
gazing at one another, all are nothing but the luminosity of the nature-jewel.

Gazing upon the pavilions from above, one beholds the crystal jewel-pools and the golden realm; amidst the air, the pavilions resound with the pure tones of celestial music, together playing the melody of non-arising.
Those who observe and listen during this enlightened time will surely attain rebirth there.
A Separate Verse on the Contemplation of Water:
An old fisherman casts his line into the depths of the blue waves; The strength of his baited hook and taut line is spent.
With a single oar beneath the clear breeze and bright moon, He knows not that his body dwells within a crystal palace.
The birds sing the Dharma;
separately they chant as the mountain fragrance wafts, filling the path. A hundred flowers nod and bow, vying in their exquisite fragrance.
The spring breeze holds boundless, profound meaning—unbeknownst to me, for whom does the yellow oriole speak?
The tree preaches the Dharma;

its distinct verses fill the palm leaves, yet not even one line can be exhausted. This single phrase, impartial toward all things, is the seal of the ten thousand dharmas and the hallmark of the thousand sages; though one’s mouth is full, it cannot proclaim it.
On the mountain ridges, the plum blossoms leak forth the news of spring’s arrival.
The general verse:
How truly marvelous! How truly marvelous! The insentient preaching the Dharma is inconceivable. If you listen with your ears, you will never understand;
only by hearing sound through the faculty of sight can you know it.
The verse begins: Born from the mind, one arises in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, sitting cross-legged within a lotus flower.
Vast and boundless, one knows not the fire; covered in dust and grime, how many years have passed? One tosses soil and stirs up sand, with no place of refuge.
In this place, he turns his body and arrives directly before the imperial palace.

Yao and Shun wear their robes with ease as the ten thousand nations pay their respects. Pushing through the clouds to see the sun, there is no need for further words. Those who come from the East sit in the East;
throughout the entire world, all are moistened by fresh rain and dew.
Pure Land Verse by Yongjue:
The Vaidūrya jewel-pool with its golden radiance— It is not in the west, nor is it in the east. When delusive thoughts are utterly extinguished, one returns to the One Buddha;
Spontaneously, one sits within the lotus flower.

Hearing these verses on the recollection of the Buddha, one learns to emulate the warbling of soaring birds. The water possesses eight meritorious qualities; its clarity reveals the pure faculty of the mind. All of this is attained through a purified heart.

Poems on Embracing the Pure Land by Yanling The lotus flowers of the Pure Land, whether near or far, leave no trace upon the path. It is only valued that one single-mindedly upholds the Buddha’s name; when the single thought is severed, all calculation is forgotten.
The six sense-gates radiate light wherever they may be. In the jeweled pond, the *padma* flowers compete to bloom; from the precious trees, the kalaviṅka birds sing.
Resonance. How many times have you traveled back and forth through this Sahā world? Only now, at this moment, do you begin to repay the efforts of your entire life.

The "Preface to the Elucidation of the Mind-Ground" in the *Contemplation Sūtra on the Infinite Life* states: "Those of the middle grade of the superior class need not necessarily uphold, receive, read, or recite the Vaipulya sūtras."

The *Dian* (Explanatory Commentary) states: "One who well understands the meaning and intent, whose mind is not startled or shaken regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), who has deep faith in cause and effect, and does not slander the Mahāyāna.
The *Miaozong* (Wondrous Commentary) says: 'Such a person upholds the meaning; they do not delight in reciting [the scriptures], but rather take up a single phrase or verse from within the sutras.'"
He profoundly exhausts the essential purport; regarding the deep and vast principle that transcends words and thought, his mind is not startled or disturbed.
Furthermore, his mind dwells securely in the Middle Way, unshaken by the two extremes. He thoroughly understands that cause and effect are both the true mark (*dharmatā*).

This is called "profound faith. Although one has not practiced universally, upon hearing the Great Teaching or encountering diverse explanations suited to different capacities, one knows they all reveal the single principle and does not give rise to doubt or slander.
This is precisely what the Chan school refers to as "investigating words that seem meaningless" to illuminate the ground of the mind.
Because such a person practices the Mahāyāna and understands the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the thousand Buddhas extend their hands to them, and they hear only the most profound teachings.

Regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*): after seven days, one attains non-retrogression; through cultivation over a minor kalpa (*antarakalpa*), one attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
As for those of the highest grade of the highest birth, they immediately realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas upon arrival;

in an instant, they pervade the ten directions and attend upon various Buddhas. If one investigates the causes of their rebirth there, they consist of maintaining the precepts, reciting and studying the Mahāyāna, and practicing cultivation.
One who practices the six recollections can perceive that the Tathāgata esteemed the precepts and the training, as well as the intent behind profound awakening;

it seems he did not wish for them to be neglected in isolation. As for Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, the Tathāgata stated that within this world, he manifested my Unsurpassed Mahāyāna Dharma—was this not the realization and clarification of the mind-ground?
It is said he attained the first Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi), yet was it not the eighth stage of a bodhisattva?
"Is it not so? he asks, and then follows it by saying, "One shall be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
This, moreover, accords with the three grades of the highest class, all of which use the great mind to turn one's merit toward rebirth; they are like two tally-sticks that fit perfectly together.

Thus Yunqi said: "Samantabhadra is the eldest son of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. Although every atom contains the Flower-Treasury World and every place is a Lotus Land, the *Caryāpraṇidhāna* chapter must..."
With earnest sincerity, they speak of rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss; yet even those who have already attained awakening remain thus, for there is nothing further to be said.
The ultimate teaching is that one awakens to the Buddha within oneself and need not seek birth [in a pure land]. This is spoken for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and above.

If it were said that those who have awakened to the primary truth (paramārtha) but have not yet severed their fetters (saṃyojana) all refrain from seeking birth [there], then they would be deluding themselves and deluding others. As the ancient masters said:
This has been explained in detail.
Chapter Seven: Verses on the Mind-Ground Revealed through the Practice of Nianfo (Buddha-Recitation). Composed by Cishou.
The trees, forests, waters, and birds each proclaim it; the jeweled nets and golden terraces are all sites of enlightenment.
If one can realize the tolling of the bell and the beating of the drum, Amitābha radiates light from his brow-hair in every place.
Verse One: Chanting in the West Originally, in the West, there was no need for manifold study; a single phrase of Amitābha is found through inward reflection.
Once one perceives one’s original true countenance, one realizes that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa.
The Buddha in the West bears the same name as I; if you directly accept this, there shall be no alarm.
If you can be awakened by a single call, what need is there for the journey of ten million billion lands?
The Western Master’s kōan has long been practiced: in profound stillness and lucid awareness, apply your mind to doubt.
When doubt reaches the point where emotion vanishes and the mind is severed, you will realize that you yourself are Amitābha.
The single phrase of the Western Land is the direct transmission; without relying on cultivation, it is already manifest before one.
If all noble beings see their nature, they shall stand shoulder to shoulder with Amitābha Buddha.
The manifold sufferings of the western realm cannot invade them. First, one must realize one's own mind and understand that the true Sukhāvatī is right before one's eyes;
when brought forth, even red earth is golden.

Traveling straight forward along the western path, one fully arouses the three minds and clearly realizes the truth of principle. By means of the highest grade of highest birth, one arrives in the snap of a finger;
upon first seeing the Buddha, one awakens to non-arising.
A Draft of Verses on the Essential Points of Mindfulness of the Buddha, spoken by the Śākyamuni of the Hermitage.
Amitābha Buddha is the body of the Dharma-realm. Furthermore, the Tiantai Master Zhiyi said:
Taking true reality (*dharmatā*) as the essence, and relying upon these two teachings as the core of the mind, then ten trillion lands will appear as if reflected in a bright mirror.
The boundless ocean of lands contains the void within its depths; this ocean and the void are entirely the Lotus Palace, and that Lotus Palace pervades everywhere throughout space.
The ocean: the empty sea alone reveals the countenance of Amitābha. Amitābha Buddha is neither born nor extinguished;

like the moon in water, difficult to grasp and difficult to seize. This body is utterly beyond words of separation. Such is the resonance, such is the teaching. I and Amitābha were originally not different;
by turning away from awakening and sinking into birth, we suddenly became separate. From this day forth, I shall sweep away all dust of emptiness and existence. Father and son [reunited].

Yet, as we have met one another, we vow to cultivate the three blessings and diligently practice the six recollections, ensuring that our actions of body, speech, and mind remain free from flaw or blemish.
Now, by means of this mindfulness of Amitābha, I shall never grow weary until I behold him face to face.
In the mind that clings to the Pure Land, one presses the eyes shut and sees flowers blooming in the void. One falsely takes the three realms to be one’s home.
Though the Great Trichiliocosm is eternally quiescent—a land of radiant light—not even a speck of dust can penetrate it; all is but obscuration.

Dragged by the ropes of craving into this suffering Sahā world, one weeps until reaching the Yellow Springs, tears ever more abundant. Who would say that the grief of parting lasts through kalpas of exhaustion?
One’s entire being is, in truth, the Ancient Amitābha.
In delusion there is no awakening; in awakening there is no delusion. Ultimately, the moment of delusion is itself the moment of awakening.
Having pulled oneself free from both extremes of delusion and awakening, the cauldron of boiling water is revealed to be a lotus pond.

The waters of the forty-eight vows merge with water; hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of spaces unite with space. The Compassionate Honored One of the Dharma-Treasury has no face or form;
there is no need to seek his countenance of purple-gold once more.
When I maintain right mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha, the shadows of the jeweled trees in the pond linger lazily in the sunlight. Yet my mind still hastens to return to the realm of purity and peace;
this is once again planting eyebrows upon my eyes.
The cycle of birth and death through ten thousand kalpas is like a grave illness; a single invocation of the Buddha’s name is the skilled physician.
When the medicine and the disease are ultimately both forgotten, there is no need for further proclamation—the mother need not remember her child.
Take the single phrase of Amitābha as the pivot; hold it alone without seeking anything else.
When the practice reaches its ultimate penetration and the lump of clay is shattered, even an iron Buddha breaks into a sweat across his entire body.
For what reason is this world called "Ultimate Bliss"? Simply because it cannot be invaded by the various sufferings.
If a seeker of the Way wishes to find the path home, they need only recognize their own mind within the midst of worldly dust.
Arising and ceasing, non-arising arising, non-arising—how could the Land of Bliss ever forbid people from walking there?
Who would have known that within ten-thousand-fathom red dust, the *padma* flower blooms at the first watch of the moon?
This mind is empty and still; upon what can thought rely? As for returning to one's native land, who has not already returned?
Beyond the flowers, the jade rooster cries at the dawn sun, welcoming the distant arrival of the Buddha and honoring his compassion.
The phases of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness are the truly pure land; seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving are the ancient Amitābha.
Simply by forgetting birth and death in this very place, father and son shall pull each other out of the river of craving.
Outside of Chan, I have never spoken of the Pure Land; you must know that outside of the Pure Land, there is no Chan.
Cast aside both layers of this public case, and the five-petaled lotus will bloom upon Mount Xionger.

Within the house of the great dream, not a single dharma exists; yet within this state of no-dharmas, a thousand differences arise. Turning back to contemplate one's own nature, one is free from discrimination;
in every thought-moment, the pure white lotus flower fully unfolds.
Within the dark chamber dwells a great black viper; do not greedily indulge in sleep before it has been driven out entirely.
With the skull-caps of the dead crushed beneath the pillow of Mount Sumeru, a fragrant breeze spreads across the earth as white lotuses bloom.
The road to one's hometown is easy to find, with no deviations; yet the bright sun and clear sky are obscured by external objects. Raise your two eyebrows and look within:
even the fiery pit is entirely white lotus flowers.

A journey of over a hundred thousand leagues does not separate one from the dust of the world. Cease using delusion and awakening to distinguish between the distant and the near. In a single kṣaṇa of thought, all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are realized;
together, they are all people within the Land of Lotus Flowers.
In the practice of Buddha-recollection, one need only strive to become a Buddha; if one does not strive to become a Buddha, what is the purpose of recollecting?
For all who possess consciousness and harbor a spirit, the white lotus is equally possessed by each as a single branch.
Manifesting entry into *nirvāṇa* and recording the second month of spring, he dances and sings before the wind, lamenting Pāpīyān.
Who would have known that the Buddha of the intrinsic nature’s golden hue constantly turns the wheel of Dharma amidst a thousand blossoms?
On this Cold Food Festival, the desolate outskirts resound with universal wailing; who among them thinks afar of the Elder Golden Immortal?
Buried in the Lotus Land at the beginning of the kalpa, he has no need for people to come and offer paper money.
In the clear and harmonious season of early summer, the fourth month, the nine dragons spray water to bathe the infant. The Master of the Land of Bliss is free from birth and death;
he simply fashions his face out of pure gold.
In the hometown of Qingtai, there are no months of the sixth lunar station; let the fire-parasols spread themselves across the void as they may.
Upon the ground of golden sand, where he once walked in meditation, gust after gust of white-lotus breezes blows forth.
Who would have known that the chrysanthemums by the eastern fence in the ninth month are none other than the four-colored flowers of the Western Paradise?
When a single skull is dried to its very end, the myriad perceptions and experiences are naturally without error.
The faculty of mindfulness is a single string of prayer beads; with pain as the whip and exertion as the goad, do not seek distant goals.
When mindfulness reaches the emptiness of mindfulness and is liberated through mindfulness, one is unaware that the body rests upon a white lotus.
The lotus fiber binds the feet of the golden crow; the fires of karma burn the chariot and the flowers. Yet there is another, even more difficult-to-believe dharma:
with the tips of one’s toes, one kicks out Buddhas as numerous as sesame seeds.
The moment one wishes to return home, one arrives at home. Why needlessly give rise to sighs of lamentation? The great road before the gate is as straight as a bowstring;
the moment one attempts to traverse the path of conceptual thought, one has already gone astray.
A single hook-shaped crescent moon illuminates the pine hermitage; outside the gate, no one dwells in the thatched hut.
The Lord of Transformation, with his billions of bodies of purple-gold, does not depart from this very thought—this is to be a fellow practitioner.
The self-nature Amitābha is beyond proof and cultivation; it requires only that one strike at oneself to find resonance.
If one glances at the present thought while maintaining subject and object, one is once again blinded by the eyes by the flowers of emptiness.
The long whale swallows in one breath, drying up the four oceans; the Amitābha of self-nature possesses a vast field of vision. The jade-white light between his brows cannot be concealed;
it is like a full moon upon a branch of coral.
In the land of Lotus Flowers there are no golden chains; yet when one hears or sees, Mount Cakravāḍa appears within the heap.
If one can penetrate through the sounds and forms before one’s eyes, hundreds of thousands of worthy sages will all return as one.

For one's livelihood, there is only the support of a single boat; drifting through the currents, stopping at any hollow, one speaks only of conditions. How many times has the ancient sail been unfurled by the bright moon?
Before one’s eyes, the lotuses of the Buddha-ocean bloom everywhere.

Dwelling on the boat while reciting the Buddha’s name, the Buddha follows the boat; the eternal, tranquil light stirs the heavens beneath the water. Neither the two banks nor the middle of the stream touch it;
branch after branch of red lotus blossoms from the field of the mind.
At dawn, the boat moved straight east; the full sails were brushed by the breeze of lotus flowers.
