The single Honored One, Amitābha Buddha of Self-Nature, appeared over the rising sun, his light glowing red before my eyes.
The mindful mind follows the body like a shadow; whether in stillness or clamor, leisure or haste, it never ceases for a moment. When the physical form is shattered, the shadow perishes with it;
in the lands of India and this Middle Kingdom, all paths are cut off.
Amitābha dwells in the West; the Patriarch came from the West. Reciting the Buddha’s name and practicing Zen share the same essential form.
Once the knot of doubt accumulated over kalpas is shattered, the flowers of the mind bloom together as one.
The lecture hall divides the schools of Characteristics and Nature; one seeks to establish characteristics while the other seeks to refute them.
Yet when we come to this lecture at the lotus pond, how could the blossoms ever be two different shades of red?
The boat comes to rest in the east, west, south, and north; yet it still does not leave the ancient sandbar. At ease, I shift the rudder of empty space;
fragrance fills the boat, and flowers fill the islet.
Breaking through empty space, laughter fills the cheeks; the wondrous, luminous treasury opens wide.
To understand the affairs prior to the void kalpa, one must take full responsibility for each and every thing as it emerges.
A Verse on Mindfulness of the Buddha:
One phrase of the *udumbara* flower—Amida, free from deluded thought. With every sound, it flows forth from one’s own mind.
If you can see through this very point, The rootless iron tree will naturally blossom.
A single phrase of Amitābha quiets ten thousand activities; the azure pool, wind-still, is profoundly serene.
At night’s depth, the moon appears in the heart of the waves, surging forth like a single pearl from a silver platter.
A single phrase of Amitābha’s roar like thunder: the eyes of the ocean of lands in the ten directions open wide. The Dharma-king’s decree is personally upheld;
both the ordinary and the holy come to take refuge.
The single phrase "Amitābha" is for those of the highest capacity; with vital energy void and spirit luminous, they penetrate deeply into the subtle mystery.
Having entered entirely into the realm of constant radiance, truly there is nothing to say—to whom could it be directed?
With one phrase of Amitābha, right faith is profound; the rare *tán-huá* flower early manifests the spring of a single branch. Clearly, this is the perfect phrase for arriving home:
the old master of the Western Land within one's own nature.
With a single phrase of Amitābha, the mind is naturally enlightened; one knows with certainty that not a single step is taken in vain.
Beneath one’s feet, Amitābha manifests; ten thousand lotus flowers spring up underfoot.
A single phrase of Amitābha is itself the sūtra; its reception and upholding require one’s own self-awakening.
The treasuries of hundreds of thousands of millions of dragon palaces are realized within a single thought-moment of the person.
In a single thought, the mind opens and one attains him; when looked for, he seems to exist, yet upon seeking, he is gone.
Although his skillful means are not many, he displays his majestic radiance, filling the great void.
Within one's own home is a single Amitābha Buddha; when you raise a thought, you do not see him. To recognize him as such still results in two;
I shall explain this to you for you, and you will laugh heartily.

The realm of true permanence and quiescence transcends all thought and deliberation; Prajñā opens its blossoms upon the field of perfect enlightenment. Herein dwell all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
a single branch of the utpala flower wafts its fragrance from within the fire.
Within the light of tranquil illumination, great capacity is revealed; Amitābha stands face-to-face, manifesting his golden body. His entire being is his hand, his entire being is his eye;
at the third watch of the midnight hour, the wooden bird cries out.
The simultaneous vanishing of stillness and illumination is truly marvelous. Illuminating heaven and earth, it is inconceivable. The stone man claps his hands and laughs aloud;
to whom can this scene of splendor be described?
Without the illumination of wisdom, meditation cannot exhaustively fathom stillness; if there is no meditation, the illumination of wisdom will not be profound.
When meditation and wisdom are perfectly integrated and unimpeded, they are like the bright moon in a clear blue sky piercing through a pure breeze.
For how many years have I contemplated Amitābha? I often thought of casting it aside to practice Chan.
Since the moment we met face-to-face, I have finally realized that the vast sky is itself the heavens.
I recall that at the assembly of Amitābha, I attained Zen; with every sound, the unmanifest before birth flows forth. The wooden man claps his hands and laughs aloud;
the one-horned mud ox sleeps at the bottom of the sea.
I call to mind Amitābha, who thunders the Dharma’s peal; The weary eyes of the dreaming world open all at once. A thousand-year-old lotus root bursts forth with fresh blossoms;
Boundless fragrant winds stir through the nine realms.
I contemplate Amitābha, who penetrates the ten directions; throughout the ten directions, he alone is the Dharma-King. Before my eyes, both the defiled and the pure are without obstruction;
even from atop a heap of refuse, he radiates light.
I recall that Amitābha was attached to signs; all sentient beings call him Amitābha, yet he has not truly realized this himself.
Nevertheless, Amitābha has nonetheless conferred upon them the prediction of enlightenment.
I recall Amitābha; my faith is surely karmically linked. Seeking the profound, I have reached the edge of Tiger Creek.
Upon the summit of the solitary peak, I open my two eyes and see clearly that the flower of the mind fills the great trichiliocosm.
I contemplate Amitābha and find abundant ease; before my eyes, I ask nothing more. Leisurely trailing my staff, I ascend the mountain to gaze afar;
Ten thousand layers of peaks gather emerald hues like coiled shells.

In a single thought, the mind is level and the Dharma-realm is level; throughout the myriad worlds of the great trichiliocosm, mounds and pits are utterly eliminated. From head to foot, every step is expedient means;
the Great Way is majestic and grand—proceed as you will.
The single volume of the True Sutra is not to be sought outside; its boundless, wondrous meanings reside within the eye of wisdom. Without ever being raised, it is known beforehand;
in a single kṣaṇa, the entire Tripitaka is complete.
The wondrous meaning of this single scroll of the True Sutra is profound; though many recite it, few truly understand it.
With every sound, the Vajra-eye breaks forth, piercing through the heart of all Buddhas of antiquity.
A single scroll of the True Scripture is brought forth through recitation; one does not know who it is that performs the recitation.
Were it not for one who clearly realizes the fundamental principle beyond the ordinary, how could one recognize the priceless treasure within the robe?
The Buddha is the Buddha with sound; meditation is the Buddha without sound. What, ultimately, are these things of sound and no-sound?
The Vajra Eye opens at the crown of the head; the fragrance of white lotuses scatters across lands as numerous as grains of sand.
Buddha-recitation and Zen meditation share the same essence; Amitābha dwells in the West, and the Patriarchs came from the West.
If one can simply break through the ball of doubt, the red lotus flowers will bloom in no way different.
All Buddhas and sentient beings are one with this. Among the four modes of birth and the six realms, who is without it? From the heavens above to the earth below, how many know it?
I ask you: who can recognize this "He"?
With faith and mindfulness, one reaches the Western Land; the lotus of the original nature blooms, its fragrance pervading the world.
Filling and breaking through all of space, it is entirely myself—there is no need to wash my face or put on clothes.
*Verses on Cherishing the Pure Land* by Chu Shi: There is an Amitābha within one’s own mind;
The moment a single thought arises, it is separated by a thousand peaks. How could one possibly turn the light back to illuminate it?
Instead, one turns directly outward to seek it. Green waters and blue mountains are all its wondrous essence; Yellow orioles and purple swallows are all [its manifestation].
Mysterious Sound: Ordinary people merely suffer because their greed and anger are heavy; they do not realize that their bodies dwell within a forest of jewel trees.

The Dharma of impermanence and non-self encompasses all; how could the water-birds, the wind, and the forest be any different? Without stirring so much as a speck of dust, one is always in meditative concentration;
though wandering through all Buddha-lands, one returns once more. Ordinary people are fundamentally identical to Maitreya; how could the wise ever be separate from them?
O Sudhana, when endurance is attained, it becomes the pure realm; the flower of awakening blooms once more upon the deluded mind.
As mountain clouds gather thickly and the waters flow coolly, they together recite a single scroll of scripture from the Western Land.

The stone tiger returns to roar beneath the crags; the clay man goes to listen amidst the trees. The wind blows the mirage, scattering with the waves; the rain drenches the flowers of emptiness as they drift away.
Ti-ling. At this moment, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is worthy of one’s stay;
where is Amitābha not manifesting his form? One has not yet recognized the preceding stages of coarse objects; how could one have ever known that which lies beyond the Dharmakāya?

Alas, in the turning of the head and twisting of the neck, one mistakenly identifies the time of offering incense and choosing firewood. Six characters are transmitted from mouth to ear; between the holy and the mundane, there is not a single separation.
Threads of silk—majestic is the True Buddha of daily life. To turn the light back in haste is already late.
Dwelling in seclusion, all is quiet; the cypress trees stand dense and tall. Let not the dust of the mundane world stain the pure breast.

One Buddha’s name encompasses infinite Buddhas; the merit of the final thought lies in the very first. When the clouds part, the white moon’s radiance fills the sky; after the rain, the green mountains reveal their topknots.
The colors are deep; one should contemplate the cessation of birth and cultivate discerning understanding. The sound of the wind and the cry of the crane are all profound tones.
If it is not through mindfulness of the Buddha, then practice Zen. When you have attained Zen, the Buddha appears before you.

The ten-thousand-fathom azure pool becomes pure from this point on; a single orb of autumn moon hangs suspended in the sky. Truly, let the inner and outer radiance penetrate through, so that all things, high and low, are seen in their entirety.
The Elephant is Complete. This Dharma King has neither going nor staying; only then does one know he does not fall into the extremes of annihilation or permanence.
I exhort practitioners of Zen:
practicing Zen is simply to clarify one's own mind. To become a Buddha, why seek it outwardly? In movement and stillness, in coming and going, the truth is ultimate.
Joy! Behold and know the ancient Avalokiteśvara. He hangs high the sun of wisdom over the three thousandfold world-system; he universally manifests the light of compassion for a million fathoms.
To grasp the root of practice, one must recite the Buddha’s name; even immortals and seers require deep application of effort.
The verse for mindfulness of the Buddha shown to [Name]:
Before you reach fifty-eight years of age, observe how many years you actually have remaining. Contemplate this with great urgency; once those years are exhausted, it will all be over.

One who has fully understood is truly mindful of the Buddha; one who has not yet understood must begin mindfulness early. Birth and death arise from the body; apart from the body, where can they be sought? Regarding the verse on birth:
"I know for myself that today I emerged from my mother’s womb; why has my mother not come today? Coming and going, one searches for the mother but finds no trace.
Attained! A single branch blooms within the Land of Lotus Flowers.

In this poem of the Pure Land, Xueqiao’s coral branch hangs like a frail rhinoceros horn. The waves tossed upon the sea of suffering have no end; one must bite through this entire mass of empty space.
Moon, let us join hands and enter the multi-storied tower.
From the *Pure Land Poems* by Boshan:
"The pure mind is itself the Western Land; Leaping across Kunlun, one enters the sea gate. Walking until the water ends and the mountains are exhausted.
This place is vividly a separate heaven and earth;
the pure mind is itself the land of the West. Not even a needle can pass through its gates, yet chariots and horses travel freely therein.
As soon as the cawing of the crows on the ancient tree has ceased, a full moon emerges, enshrouded in mist.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West. A wooden horse neighs as it passes through Han and Qin. Treading upon skulls, who is there to be the master?
Old acquaintances from many years ago are all renewed at once.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; within the light of formlessness lies the body with form.
When mind and objects entangle one another, they become a ghostly play; who is the "I," and who is the "person"?
A pure mind is itself the land of the West; The pillar and the lantern laugh without ceasing.
Having exhausted all the bitter flavors of the world, Upon the meditation cushion, a lingering fragrance remains.
A pure mind is itself the land of the West; one must know that beyond the teachings there is a separate path to tread.
If you are a guest at the gate of the Patriarchs, a radiant smile is truly beyond the discussion of non-arising.
A pure mind is the Western Land; does the skin-sack still know pain and itch? What realm is it that turns heaven and earth upside down?
Beyond the night-bright curtain lies the night-luminous pearl.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West; meeting in appearance, a raised eyebrow or a lowered brow suffices. The ancient path leaves no trace of carriage or horse;
the tongue, boneless, is surely the compass needle.
The pure mind is itself the land of the West. When the realm of Māra is empty, the realm of the Buddha is empty. The drifting clouds of the world are gathered and exhausted;
a single orb bursts forth, painting the sea and heavens crimson.

A pure mind is itself the land of the West. Joining the ranks and following the crowds, I provide gruel and rice for the Sangha; once sated, there is no concern other than the healing of hunger’s sores.
With earnest devotion, I offer lamps before the Buddha.
A pure mind is the land of the Western Paradise; in an ancient temple, serene and secluded, the moon shines through the window. At midnight, a mouse is caught beside the bed;
at dawn, it flies out as a pair of embroidered mandarin ducks.
Dedication for the Pure Land Poems:
I, Yu, gaze afar upon the Great Teacher of the West; Last night the moon emerged from the coral branches. The Song of Non-arising has been fully blown through the Jade Capital;
It is precisely the time when the superior lotus blooms.
Clouds dwell in deep mountains; cranes reside in the woods. My heart finds its refuge only in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.
Tonight, as the moon shines upon the long corridor, a single phrase of Amitābha resonates like a sound beyond kalpas.
In autumn mountains, I seek solitude without a companion; ancient halls and cold cliffs grow deeper with every step. A single phrase of Amitābha echoes through the distant valleys;
the empty forest and stubborn rocks seem like those who understand my heart.
Calling it a wave or calling it a ripple, both are but water; dividing them into Chan or into worldly affairs—how could these be different paths?
Not realizing that the Buddha-dharma is not something manifold, one vainly pursues names and words, falling into the extremes of existence and non-existence.
Sitting cross-legged at midnight, a single stroke of the bell rings out; it shatters the West, leaving no trace behind. Only then do I realize that Amitābha was originally myself;
drawing back the curtain, the moon shines upon ten thousand layered peaks.
Sometimes I ascend alone to the peak of a solitary mountain, gazing afar toward the west as my home. A few wisps of white cloud emerge from distant peaks;
a flight of sparse geese passes across the edge of the sky.
A Verse on Avalokiteśvara’s Perfect Penetration:
Seeking the Master within the Purple Bamboo Grove, I mistakenly entered the Perfect Penetration, which is no ordinary place. A few wisps of white cloud drink from the green waters;
A single orb of red sun breathes forth from the green mountains.
The *liu* flowers emerge freshly washed by the rain; the birds' songs from amidst the clouds carry the tide. Alone I pity these tidings that no one recognizes;
several times I have donned my straw raincoat to transplant bamboo.
The reeds stand in deep shadow as the autumn waters darken; the traveler, without companion, feels increasingly desolate.
If you examine that moment when every thought stirs with alarm, you will find it is none other than Avalokiteśvara who hears the sound and beholds the world.
A carbuncle on one's back may be compared to an almsbowl; a stye on one's face may resemble a peach. One need only consider what lies within—who knows the pain?
Do not ask about the perfect penetration of the white jade brow-hair.
Death after death, life after life, born again and dying; coming and going, departing and returning. Within the ranks of the Universal Gate (Samantamukha), there is no coming or going;
amidst the thicket of birth and death, one beholds Sudhana.

In spring, the orioles sing throughout the willow-smoke cities; in autumn, when the wild geese cry, the reeds sound white. One cannot finish listening to the hundred birds and their hundred voices—what need is there to further inquire about the sound of the ocean tide?
When hand touches hand, each has its own awareness; do not harbor doubt regarding this message.
Of the eighty-four thousand arms of Great Compassion, try to see who lacks even a single one.
The porcupine’s needle-spikes can cover its entire body; the snail’s palace follows it wherever it goes. With green steps and white walls, all is peace and joy;
falling flowers, fragrant breezes—all are spring.

The firefly’s light within its belly is like a candle; the buzzing of mosquitoes upon their wings is as long as a symphony of pipes and strings. Since these pleasures accompany one wherever one goes, they are fit for enjoyment at all times;
there is no need to ask others where one's hometown lies.
How wondrous it is that his four hooves tread upon the earth; how serene it is that his two horns prop up the heavens.
Moving in and out with absolute freedom and without hindrance, he rides backward upon a donkey to the cloud-topped peaks.
On the branches, the feathered tribes form a palace; beneath the earth, the masses of grass create a grotto-chamber. Do not say that dwelling in seclusion has its high and low places;
the vast sky and empty valley share but one autumnal light.
The ant-hill is intricate, as if wrought by spirits; layer upon layer, they connect in dense interpenetration.
When the minute dust-body enters the minute dust-earth, recognize that it is one with the Treasury of Light.
Pure Land Poem by Huì:
The crimson wheel is certain to sink in the west; I wonder not where the soul now dwells. Pánshān’s realization was nothing other than this:
the filial son is originally Dàláng.
The moon reflects in the lotus pond, and the pond reflects the sky; the wind sounds through the bamboo and trees, and the trees sound with the wind.
How many extraordinary men in this world have mistaken Amitābha for being on some distant peak!
Pure Land Verse:

Tracing the Source The origins of my drifting traces are recorded with clear distinctness. Within stillness, do not allow discursive thoughts to arise. Cut off the path of coming and going, of birth and death;
there is no need to contend for the lands of one’s native home.
The Pure Land Verses by Shen Lang:
Borrowing human sentiments, I say that the waves of the dregs of the Dharma are perilous; do not look upon Amitābha with indifferent eyes.
When recitation reaches the point of sudden, direct encounter, it is like speaking of Chang’an from within the Han-yuan Palace.
The Verses on the Subtle Intention that All Buddhas and Tathāgatas are the Body of the Dharma Realm, Entering into the Minds and Thoughts of All Sentient Beings.
Heaven and earth are entirely a land of gold; all phenomena are the complete, pure, and wondrous body. The jade maiden turns her back to the wind, yet there is neither front nor back;
the numinous sprout transforms into elegance, unaware of spring.
The verse says: When one contemplates the Buddha in the mind, this very mind is the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs;
in the four directions, above, and below, there is no obstruction. It wells forth like a crystal pitcher into the azure sky, containing the six within its unperforated shell.
The Vinaya: A single note of *kuan-nai* passes over the distant river;
meeting beyond the eons, one travels to the other shore. Within the thicket of numinous sprouts, the iron ox plows; the east wind scatters the snow from a thousand crags.
Lying empty upon the cloudless sky, the solitary moon shines bright.
This verse is the Buddha;

this mind is the Buddha—this is the plain and honest deliberation upon which the title is based. To pour out the entire dish is not a matter of stinginess. Look tonight at the bright star of the night;
behold it as it reveals its very breast. Observe it with careful attention.

The Buddha and sentient beings are fundamentally not different; it is only to guide those lost on the ford that one speaks of "attaining Buddhahood. Like using yellow leaves to stop a child’s crying, there is truly no other way;
once awakened from the dream, one first recognizes the old acquaintance.
A few wisps of white cloud span the valley mouth; before the curtain, a rain of flowers, unaware of spring.
Picking up the spoon and grasping the chopsticks as if fully awakened, sweeping the floor and burning incense without asking another.
The ocean of the Buddhas’ perfect and universal wisdom arises from the mind’s perceptions;
A heron’s nest, a dewdrop, a dream just returning. A crescent moon like a half-hook rises over ten thousand households; From where does this single white cloud arise?
The child of the white cloud leans against its father, the green mountain.
Not a single thin cloud appears; the misty waves stretch wide. The white birds have all flown away, and the azure sky returns.
Having worn through his straw sandals until their heels are broken, He sits majestically upon Mount Daxiong.
The verse says: Those who behold the mark of the white tuft between the eyebrows will naturally see the eighty-four thousand marks and secondary characteristics manifest within a single hair-tip;
the message is communicated throughout the entire realm, luminously clear and unrevealed. When stillness reaches its ultimate limit, it bursts open from the crown of the head.
The eye: within the gateway of worldly toil, all is golden light.
When one penetrates through for oneself, one knows for oneself; of the eighty thousand rays of light, who else need be asked? To take it up as a whole is to see it as a whole;
atop the summit of Mount Sumeru, one bears Mount Sumeru.

Verse on the Middle Birth of the Superior Grade (Not necessarily upholding, reciting, or reading the Vaipulya sutras; yet well-understanding their meaning and intent, their minds are not startled or shaken regarding the ultimate truth [paramārtha-satya]. They are received by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas upon a purple-golden platform like a great precious lotus, universally hearing all sounds purely expounding the ultimate truth).
Do not seek the fundamental truth in the title of a sutra; what is the point of searching for the body of the Dharma King amidst a stack of paper?
If you can take up the responsibility before the palm-leaf manuscript is even opened, you will avoid becoming a person who merely traces the lines and counts the characters.

The foolish child clings to the money meant to stop his crying; the fine steed chases the wind, looking back at its shadow as it strikes the whip. As clouds sweep across the vast sky, the crane nests in the moon;
a cold clarity pierces to the very bone, and sleep cannot come.
What was accomplished by facing the wall for so long? How could one hope to open the mind and see the original source?
Since the empty kalpa, all sons of the Buddha have attained spontaneous perfection without even raising a *huatou*.
Regarding the *Pure Land Verses*, Master Ouyi of Boshan, whenever he expounded upon them, would say: "A pure mind is itself the land of the West.
This was intended to encompass the effect within the cause; yet readers failed to grasp this, leading them to subsume phenomena under principle. I have personally encountered such instances.

Moved by these reflections, I have further taken up the Western [Pure Land] as being precisely the land of the mind-only (*cittamātra*). This is intended to support principle through phenomena, so that the principle does not fall into a biased emptiness.
I do not dare to surpass the predecessors; I merely offer this as a humble contribution to the task of correcting imbalances and remedying defects.
The West is precisely the land of Mind-only; to speak of Mind apart from the land is truly perverse.
Every thought-moment returns entirely to the ocean of the Buddhas—why seek the Zen of the Patriarchs anew?
The West is precisely the land of Mind-only; only when principle and phenomena correspond does one begin to achieve merit.
If in daily life one cannot yet avoid the activity of phenomenal manifestation, how can one recklessly attempt to emulate the True Doctrine?

The Western Quarter is precisely the land of Mind-Only; when the land is pure and the mind is empty, even illness is forgotten. There is no need to laboriously seek the excellent medicine from without;
the single flavor of *agada* leaves a lingering fragrance.
Demonstrate the cultivation of pure karma and awaken eternally;

maintain mindfulness with constant, dense diligence. How could arising and ceasing ever become a single mass? When mindfulness reaches the point where arising and ceasing do not interfere with one another, the lotus flower constantly appears beneath one's feet.

Other Buddhas are clearly none other than one's own Buddha; to contemplate another is the same as contemplating oneself. When one morning, in silent contemplation, one forgets both self and other, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is gathered back within the eastern courtyard of the west.
Do not say that the West lacks the Land of Ultimate Bliss; it is simply because here there is this Sahā world.
Once you have shattered this Sahā world into powder, the West will not be separated by so much as a single speck of dust.

The Sahā world of the five turbidities is originally empty; it is only due to deluded attachment that one is imprisoned within its confines. Empty flowers appear as real, yet they have neither arising nor ceasing;
their brilliant display is entirely due to the cataracts in one's eyes.
In the verse on mindfulness of the Buddha:

"The practitioner of mindfulness of the Buddha must focus on the exhalation alone, yet must also attend to the inhalation. With a pure mind continuing in succession, the clouds of obstruction disperse;
touch the tip of your own nose as it was before birth."

Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha must ensure their minds are diligent and not lax. From time immemorial, deluded emotions have long persisted; yet if one can rouse oneself with a single resolute thought and remain thus at all times, the precious lotus will radiate light day after day.

One who practices the mindfulness of the Buddha must resolve with the persistence of a single drop of water; one must know that even stone can be pierced through. When the thought of mindfulness bursts forth like a fire-drill striking heaven, what need have they for the five-colored lotuses of the Western Paradise?
Those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha must be upright and sincere; only then can they achieve right faith.
Thus they cultivate the seeds of Bodhi within themselves and become true spiritual heirs of Amitābha.
To the friends of the Pure Land Society, I show:
A single thought of Amitābha is like solid iron; whether in leisure or toil, in motion or stillness, it is free from birth and extinction.
This land and the Western Paradise both turn to dust—what need is there to speak of "non-arising," which is like snow in a boiling cauldron?
A single phrase, towering like a vajra, has refused to be forgotten despite a hundred refinements and a thousand hammer-strokes. It penetrates directly beyond the limit of Aeon-Long Sound;
without departing from the square inch of one's own mind, one is in the Western Paradise.
Where the sword-wheel is brandished, the night-light grows cold; the mountain colors and the sound of the stream cannot deceive.
One must wait until the golden cock personally heralds the dawn, when the five-colored lotuses reflect upon the jeweled balustrade.
Holding the name requires no further seeking of the profound; with a single phrase, one instantly transcends sound and form.
When the myriad realms merge into a single moon, how can one distinguish between the East and the West?
When will this deluded madness of outward pursuit ever end? Even if one piles up mountains of gold, one only piles up sorrow.
If you are willing to let go of everything with total sincerity, the autumn moon will shine upon a cloudless, vast sky.

Gather all six sense faculties into mindfulness of the Buddha alone; once superficial emotions are fully refined away, realization is spontaneously perfected. Upon the towering pedestal, the golden countenance is present;
there is no need to give rise to a thought, for it is naturally clear.
Do not give rise to likes or dislikes toward external conditions; when concentrated into a single thought, there is ultimately no division.
Suddenly shatter the lapis lazuli mirror, and the sound of the Dharma will be heard by you alone.
The Pure Land Verse:
Each person possesses their own ancient Amitābha; do not let it slip away during the twelve hours of the day.
If you simply ensure that the light of the mind is never obscured, there is no need to snap your fingers to leave this Sahā world.
One hundred verses on the virtuous friends who guide those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha:
When ignorance is raised up with a single sound, that very sound is intimate. With every sound raised up, the true person manifests.
When the mist disperses and the clouds dissolve, the autumn moon is bright; the ocean and sky are vast and open, white as silver.
Amitābha and you have been bitter enemies; saliva drips from the corners of your mouth as you scold him incessantly.
Suddenly, when the true eye opens wide, you will finally know that every step treads upon the lotus boat.

Upon hearing this verse for recollecting the Buddha, I learned that you possess the aspiration for the Pure Land. Only by awakening to the mind does one know the land; within the realms and paths, there are golden cords. At the six periods of the day, do not mistake the way.

Mindfulness of the Buddha is mindfulness of one’s own mind; the essence of mindfulness is fundamentally empty and still. When mindfulness arises, there is nothing upon which to rely; in every thought-moment, there is no Buddha separate from the mind.
In this poem on contemplating the Pure Land: The hidden heavens and earth are all my thatched hut;
The sun and moon are ever suspended as a lamp within a single niche. When all manifold differences are melted away, there is no difference at all.

Entering the Way, one realizes that the myriad phenomena are fellow practitioners; this defiled land, born of karmic response, must be abandoned, while the Pure Land, which is but the mind, should be joyfully embraced.
The four characters of Amitābha exhaust the very depths of reality; before the kalpas began, the ancient udumbara flower bloomed.
In this poem on the Pure Land, the phoenix soars;
one must seek the joy of dhyāna away from the clamor. It is clear that from the beginningless past until now, we have known that all phenomena with form are empty and illusory;
thus the mountains are not high, and the waters are not deep.
The source from which the flow emerges has turbid water; I ask you, where can one find the unborn? Floating clouds originally lie beyond the blue sky;
it is only because the blind cannot see clearly.
A heavy ship laden with treasures rides upon the long wind; heading westward, do not err by going east. Most bitter is it when one undergoes annihilation therein;
even if iron shoes are worn through, they are of no avail.

All phenomena return to the Gate of Non-duality. Yesterday night, this evening, and again at dusk— If you wish to achieve contemplation through Prajñā, you will only then believe that spiritual powers rely upon the six sense faculties.
Exhorting to Mindfulness of the Buddha:

Chen Zhidong’s Youxiu asked, "Who says that mindfulness early is late? To mindfully recollect even in old age is not considered tardy. At the moment one turns the head of thought back, it is clearly the time of awakening from a dream."
Pure Land Verse:

Congratulating Shouchang on his journey west to pay homage to the Buddha—what cause for sorrow? With one phrase of Amitābha, he reaches the ultimate end; Wisdom suddenly unfolds, birth and death are transcended;
The path to the Lotus Land is found at the Azure Lotus Tower.

When the flowers open and one beholds the Buddha, there are eighty-four thousand marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Within these marks, there are likewise eighty-four thousand secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). Within these secondary characteristics, there are also eighty-four thousand rays of light.
The reason they are all said to be eighty-four thousand is that when the Buddha dwelt among the realm of ordinary beings, he possessed these eighty-four thousand [qualities].
Regarding the four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), within these very afflictions one perceives the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of reality.

Since the wisdom of principle and the phenomena have already merged, one is thus able to manifest eighty-four thousand marks, signs, and radiances. If a practitioner realizes that the mind itself is the Buddha, they can perceive the true mark within all afflictions.
As a sutra says: "The Buddha observes that within the minds of all sentient beings, amidst their afflictions, there exists [the Tathāgata]."
The manifested body sits in the full lotus posture, solemn and motionless, endowed with all marks of excellence. Tiantai says:

"The Dharma-body of all Buddhas is of the same substance as one's own. That which appears within the mind when contemplating the Buddha is precisely the very substance of the Dharma-bodies of all Buddhas."
This means that this very mind is Buddha; Buddha arises from contemplation. This means that this very mind creates Buddha.

The practitioner should, according to the principle that this Buddha is the creation of Buddha, achieve perfect illumination in a single thought-moment. Through contemplation, one sees the Buddha; once this contemplation has become mature, [the realization is complete].
The Sūtra states: "Amitāyus Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta constantly come to the place where this practitioner dwells.
The *Miaozong* (Profound Commentary) says: "The moment of mindfulness is itself the point of arrival; therefore, one is able to anticipate future events.
Furthermore, because the essence of the Buddhas and sentient beings is not distinct, these three sages 'come' even though they do not come. Thus, at the time of the end of life..."
That one sees the Buddha upon the blossoming of the lotus is likewise an ordinary and familiar occurrence.
Furthermore, Wang Longshu said: "There are those who doubt how people here [in this world] can appear within the Western Seven-Jeweled Pond."
Immediately, a single lotus flower sprang forth. He replied: "Objects within a great bright mirror appear naturally as they come.
Since the land of Amitābha Buddha is pure and luminously clean, how could it not clearly reflect the worlds of the ten directions?
Furthermore, some doubt whether the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions can know those who recite the Buddha's name at the moment of death and come to welcome them. He replied:"
If a single day in heaven illuminates the entire world, how much more so the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha! The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"If one can recollect the Buddha with an unmoving mind, one will constantly behold immeasurable Buddhas. If one constantly beholds immeasurable Buddhas, one will see that the essence of the Tathāgata is eternally abiding.
Now, if sentient beings who recollect the Buddha can thus see the Tathāgata, how could there be any instance where the Tathāgata is unable [to be seen]?
Do you see sentient beings? Sentient beings with evil karma can see the hells; how could those with pure mindfulness fail to see the Tathāgata?
This is the eighth [point]: seeing the Buddha as the flowers bloom.
In the Pure Land Poem by Pang Daoxuan:
"The ten directions are all equal; this is the True Suchness Temple. Within it dwells Amitābha, who originally has no name."
Ordinary people do not enter into the principle; their minds dwell upon worldly affairs. They beg for money to purchase tiles and timber to roof over empty spaces.
Thus driven by the six thieves, they turn their backs on true suchness-wisdom, enduring hardship all day long while vainly plotting for fame and profit.
For such a practitioner of the Way, even after many kalpas, they will ultimately not fail to reach it. The four natures are one dwelling; the three bodies are one chamber.
All evil associates are seen as Amitābha Buddha. Though the description of phenomena fills the world, upon entering into principle, there is truly nothing more.
Constantly bound by conditioned existence, on what day shall one behold Amitābha? When the single thought-moment is pure, lotus flowers bloom everywhere;
in each flower is a pure land, and in each land is a Tathāgata.
A Poem on Being Born in the Pure Land at the Hour of Death:
The Immortal Pond has never had a home from which to return; Amidst the clouds, who knows the path that leads there?
The light of the stream falls afar upon the moon of the western mountains— This is precisely the moment when the dream of the Immortal Pond ends.
Half a month before his passing, he saw verses and a lattice of a thousand flowers in the void;
in a dream, he beheld a lotus pond of seven treasures. Having firmly trodden the path back to the West, he was free from even a single trace of doubt.

Exhorting the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name with compassion, ten thousand people of like mind took up the invocation of Amitābha. Through the mutual support of the multitude, their power of aspiration grew great; they personally beheld the Buddha upon a single lotus flower.
Only then did they realize that the Pure Land surpasses this Sahā world.
Verse on Rebirth in the Pure Land, No.
1: I, Xingwu, am ninety years old; my hair is as white as snow. In this world, there should be no guest who reaches a hundred years. Xingwu, the Way-man, returns home;
seated upon the golden terrace, heaven and earth are constricted.
In the north, facing the Pure Land, the mountains surge and expand;
amidst the void, celestial music stirs. The sound of flutes and pipes is subtle, carried by the winds of heaven. It receives ordinary beings and leads them back to the assembly of the sages.
On this very day, the manly spirit is finally honored and exalted.
The script of the Western Land is perfected; the Eastern India is destroyed. A single star flies away across a thousand-flower world. Do not marvel that the spirit and soul depart so swiftly;
the Land of Bliss lies within this very cohabitation.

In the Eight Virtues Pond, the waters are deep and the lotuses vast; sitting upright in the full-lotus posture, borne upon a lotus flower, he listens to the sound of the Dharma with his ears and awakens to its meaning in his heart.
From this moment forth, he has leaped out from the confines of the womb.
The eighteen great worthies sat beneath the assembly; their work accomplished, they rode upon the five-colored clouds to the West. Where do all those people of supreme goodness now dwell?
Gathered together, they speak only of the discourse on non-arising.
The trees lining the pond’s edge do not fully conceal it; the swaying golden bridge reveals its slanting half.
Suddenly, one beholds newly born sons of the Buddha, as the *piṅgala* birds clamor where the red lotuses bloom.
Verse One for Recitation in the West:
In the precious lotus that blooms within the Western Pond, Adorned with jewels, it appears spontaneously through transformation.
Amidst the radiance of a hundred treasures, I behold the Buddha in person, Majestically seated upon a jeweled flower pedestal.
In the Pure Land of the West there are lotus wombs; I universally exhort all sentient beings to go there. With a single thought the flower opens and one personally beholds the Buddha;
forever free from the eight difficulties and the three calamities.
Within the Pure Land I cherish, peaks reflect the waters of eight virtues over sands of gold; towers of a hundred jewels scatter the morning mists.
Yet there is yet another most wondrous thing: red lotuses bloom, as large as wagons.
Spontaneously moving the boat across the waters to the south, there is no need to seek fellow practitioners elsewhere. Within one's own home is Amitābha Buddha;
in every thought-moment, the *utpala* flower blooms.

A Hymn to Amitābha: The Great Teaching of Amitābha flourishes in the Western Land; His wondrous salvation of sentient beings is immeasurable. The lotuses of the nine grades bloom, extending his invitation;
Seven layers of jade trees stand in fragrant rows. Sublime is his golden form, dignified and beautiful; Brilliant is the silver terrace, radiantly shining.
The radiant light blazes forth. Before the Hall of Great Enlightenment, he prostrates with earnest devotion; suddenly he clarifies his original nature and awakens to the True Constant.

From the *Pure Land Poems* by Boshan: "The pure mind is itself the land of the West; only upon reaching it personally can one discern the ancestral source. He has drunk dry the clear river and stands tall in his realization.
The eye is like a mirror reflecting the red sun at the bottom of clear water;
the pure mind is itself the Western Land. The bright jewel atop the fleshly crown need not be sought through personal effort.
Ten thousand people reach this path with a single snap of the fingers—do not let such a favorable moment go to waste.
A pure mind is itself the land of the West; when meeting people on a narrow path, they speak of their long and shortcomings. When both ears are deaf, hearing is all the better;
who then can distinguish the *gong* and *shang* notes of one's native dialect?
This verse reveals the wondrous way the mind becomes Buddha:
when the water of the mind enters the water, there is no distinct flavor. Thrown into space, it sinks into the void without distinction;
amidst bubbles, flowers, and reflections, the thousand-fathom waves are themselves the Lotus Prajñā Pond.

The path across a thousand cliffs is severed, yet its end is not reached; who would have known that even an iron wall can be penetrated? One’s entire body is the illness, one’s entire body is the medicine;
in a dream, one mounts a blue phoenix and enters the Vermilion Palace.
Mountains long and waters distant, we but remember each other in emptiness; Yellow leaves blown by the wind, doubts arise within my dreams.
When you see the true countenance of your own father and mother, How could meeting them be like being a foster child?
The plow-ox turns up ancient gold; its light illuminates the earth, making the mountains and peaks grow cold.
Though Wen Shu holds the nobility of the Son of Heaven, Zi Ling regards him only as an old friend.
Verse on the Highest Birth of the Highest Grade:

(Possessing all precepts and practices; reading and reciting the Mahāyāna; practicing the six mindfulnesses and dedicating merit toward rebirth; Amitābha Buddha emits great radiance and, together with various Bodhisattvas, extends his hand to welcome them; at the snap of a finger, they attain rebirth and immediately realize non-arising;
the Buddhas of the ten directions bestow predictions upon them, and they obtain the gates of dhāraṇī.)

Pure gold, refined a hundred times, reveals its full efficacy; when understanding and practice correspond, all Buddhas are one and the same. Do not marvel that they have traversed the affairs of the ten directions;
without even a snap of the fingers, behold the soaring dragon.
Shown to Zheng Yongbi: The eternal awakened mind is the Pure Land; it is pure of itself.
This principle is difficult to alter in ten thousand ways. There is no separate dharma for purifying the mind; a single Buddha dispels all doubts.
If the lotus fiber has not yet been severed, it can still pull a great elephant along. Only when even a single thought ceases can it be called the time of seeing the Buddha.
I urge you to practice mindfulness of the Buddha;
Chen Zhitang is already on the path to the Western Paradise. The clarity is right before your eyes; when the flower blooms, you shall see the Buddha. At this point, you must remain firm in heart.
Preface to the Extensive Deliverance of Sentient Beings:

When Amitābha Buddha was a bhikṣu, after he had made his forty-eight vows, he took birth among all sentient beings, assuming their physical forms and mastering their languages in order to establish his teachings. Thus, from the celestial emperors above...
Down to the most minute insects and ants, all take birth therein;
even if one were to spend immeasurable kalpas explaining this, it remains the cause for Amitābha Buddha’s attainment of Buddhahood. It is attained through a single birth alone.
When Śākyamuni was the Rishi Suprabuddha, he hired Gopī with five hundred silver coins to offer five stalks of flowers to Dīpaṃkara Buddha. Gopī asked why he was offering the flowers to the Buddha.
"What do you wish to accomplish? He replied, "I wish to achieve all-encompassing wisdom (sarvākārajñatā) and deliver all sentient beings.

This was the beginning of Śākyamuni Buddha’s initial vow; it is simply a single instance of such a resolve. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* records that when Samantabhadra Bodhisattva exhorted Sudhana, he said:
"As far as the realm of space extends, as far as the realm of sentient beings extends, as far as the karma of sentient beings extends..."
When the afflictions of sentient beings are exhausted, my vows will likewise be exhausted.

Yet, because the realm of empty space and the karma and afflictions of sentient beings can never be exhausted, my sovereign vow is likewise without end. It continues from moment to moment in uninterrupted succession;
my physical, verbal, and mental actions are never weary or fatigued, until the very last instant of my final passing, when all my faculties [dissolve].

All shall utterly disintegrate; only this King of Vows shall not forsake me. May the King of Vows guide me to be reborn in the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), where I may behold Amitābha Buddha and be born within a lotus flower.

Having received the Buddha’s prediction of enlightenment, may I rescue sentient beings from the great ocean of afflictions and suffering, enabling them all to attain rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss. This is the Great [Avataṃsaka Sūtra].
I vow only to deliver all sentient beings so that they may all be reborn in the World of Ultimate Bliss.

The "Chapter on Dedication" (*Pariṇāmanā-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "In those perilous places such as the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of King Yama, I shall offer my own body as collateral to ransom all sentient beings in the evil destinies, causing them to attain liberation from this great ocean of suffering of afflictions."

This refers to the matter of rescuing sentient beings from within [saṃsāra]. Thus, seeking to attain Buddhahood and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land are both for the purpose of delivering sentient beings.

Therefore, although those who have not yet been born in the Pure Land lack the complete vessel for delivering beings and cannot follow along with all sentient beings through birth and death, they nevertheless take the vessel of Amitābha as their own vessel.
This is a practice that can deliver others across [to liberation]. The Vow of Amitābha states: "Sentient beings of the ten directions who invoke my name shall certainly be born in my land;

even those in the realms of hell and hungry ghosts shall be born in my realm. Yunqi said: "The single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha universally accords with the capacities of sentient beings in the six paths.
When the Buddha gathers in sentient beings through his unconditioned compassion, he enters the nature of sentient beings as his own internal essence."

Regarding "perfuming" (*vāsanā*): manifesting the body to preach the Dharma constitutes external perfuming. Thus, exhorting others to recite the Buddha’s name is the meaning of external perfuming through which one beholds the Tathāgata.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "One benefits all sentient beings precisely by making it one's own practice for purifying karma."
The Ninth Verse on Extensively Delivering Sentient Beings:
A Text for Reciting the Name of Amitābha Buddha to Form One Hundred Thousand Karmic Connections.

Lord Wen Gong of Ju knew that your courage was as vast as heaven; he wished for you to form one hundred thousand connections with the Western Land, rather than seeking survival for a single body alone.
Plan: Let us all board the ferry at the riverhead together.
Verse One: Western Pure Land A single snap of the fingers in the West awakens one to non-arising;
In the superior grade, one attains Buddhahood early upon the Golden Terrace, Beholding Amitābha face-to-face and receiving his direct instruction.
Record: He shall preach the Dharma hereafter to transform the multitudes of sentient beings.

In the Western Land, he makes no distinction between the wealthy and the poor; he does not select among the wise and the foolish, the noble and the humble; he does not inquire whether one is male or female, old or young;
nor does he differentiate between monastics and laypeople, or enemies and kin.
In the West, the water of merit leaves no trace; to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, one must first reach the fundamental root.
Not only do human beings attain birth in the Pure Land, but even the crawling and wriggling insects receive its grace.
Praise for Amitābha in Verse by Ding Zhu.
The monk Zhu abandoned his wife and children to become a disciple of the Tathāgata. He recruited ten thousand people to form a Pure Land assembly.
Ding Zhu, a local resident, praised him with these verses.
When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure; the Dharma King does not speak falsely. Having extracted oneself from the dust and defilements, one has already manifested as a lotus within the fire.

Without giving rise to a single thought of arising or ceasing, the Land of Ultimate Bliss appears before one. The great trichiliocosm shares this same realm; how could it be limited to the karmic conditions of ten thousand people?

Within the Pure Land of my heart, the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence fill as many as the sands of the Ganges. It is solely because of a single initial lapse of thought that beings fail to return their gaze and reflect inward to receive deliverance;
thus they transcend birth into the Pure Land, taking refuge upon lotus flowers.
I maintain that the single phrase "Amitābha" is sufficient; there is no other dharma to be contemplated.
Clearly and directly pointing out the path home, may the fourfold assembly together ascend to the field of Great Enlightenment.
This universal exhortation to mindfulness of the Buddha is for those who have deeply entered the *utpala* gate of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Exhausting the profound mystery and reaching the ultimate stillness, its wondrous nature is difficult to conceive. Within the hollow of a lotus fiber, a hidden treasury is opened;
to save beings and benefit all life, there is no end to its period.
The gate of mindfulness of the Buddha is like a great ferryboat; it ferries people across without discriminating between the wise and the foolish.
If you know that the winds and waves on this side are perilous, you should board the boat immediately to cross to the other shore.
When the Way-man comes to the home of the Way-person, there is one stick of fragrant incense and a cup of tea;
they do not speak of worldly or mundane affairs, but with every voice they praise only the white lotus flower.
When this single scroll of the True Sutra is recited, its boundless merit is inconceivable;
the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, all turn their merit toward enlightenment, and all sentient beings within the great earth find the path home.
All sentient beings are free from the karma of killing; where in the ten directions could a blade or a block for slaughter arise? In every house and every household, all practice goodness;
exhort one another to mindfulness of Amitābha and repay the four debts of gratitude.

The sacred texts of the single treasury are not concealed; like the brilliance of stars and the clarity of the moon, they shine forth with majestic dignity. Without obscuration before one’s eyes, they are personally brought forth;
let all who know this truth join together in praise.
The single phrase of Amitābha is the gateway to transformation; how could it be restricted to cities or villages?
Even if those with false views should hear it, it will surely fall upon their sounds and enter their faculty of hearing.

A single phrase of Amitābha contains manifold roots of goodness; even the wriggling and crawling insects receive its grace. Should those in the three miserable realms or the hells hear it but once, they shall all abandon suffering and return to the gate of liberation.

In the Pure Land school of Huaijin, Master Chu’s hymns of praise for the Buddha value direct expression. To heap together flowers and cluster brocade is but a vain pursuit of novelty. Naturally moist and lustrous, they fill his physical vessel;

countless rays of light surge from the wheel of his tongue. These adornments accord with his nature as he transforms his environment; according to the capacities of beings, he exhorts them to inspire faith.
O person of mind, you who seek the waters within the pool of merit, may you completely wash away the dust upon the Sahā world.

As for those who advise on the lute, practicing the Way is like playing the lute; clarity and turbidity, high and low notes, are all matters of the mind. When the sound is too hurried, the strings are again...

The sound ceases; as soon as the finger is withdrawn, the resonance sinks back into stillness. Not a speck of dust reaches the mountain facing the door; ten thousand clamors vanish together as the moon fills the forest.
Cast aside the lute and diligently recite the Buddha’s name; Ziqi may not necessarily be a true connoisseur of music.

I urge the woodcutter to let go in an instant upon the precipice. When the tree falls and the vines wither, it is but rotten firewood. The entire mountain and river are turned back into one's own self;
all wind and moonlight are entrusted to a mind of equanimity. Upon the shoulder there is naturally a weight of a thousand *qun*; beneath the feet there has never been a single [grain of dust].
The lines are unconventional. For a woodcutter such as this, true mindfulness of the Buddha is sufficient; there is no need to pre-arrange a lotus pedestal.
I exhort those who dwell in the mountains:
for one living in seclusion, mindfulness of the Buddha is most profound. Fish leap in the clear depths, birds warble in the forest—such is the true realm of the Land of Bliss.

The realms are naturally such that day after day the body and mind are at ease. Snowy plum blossoms vie to release jade from their branches; frost-covered oranges compete to hang gold beneath their leaves.
Amitābha appears in every dust mote and land, yet sentient beings mostly seek him only toward the west.
Pure Land Verse by Bo Shan:
The pure mind is itself the Western Land; Rain falling and clouds rising, how exceptionally wondrous!
This single skeleton, clear and distinct— I raise my voice so that everyone may know.
To the Reverend Shida Li: Awakening is eternal;
proceeding toward the Western Land is exceedingly easy. One only fears that the ordinary mind refuses to rest. When the ordinary mind is fully stilled, one returns to perfect enlightenment;
this very mind is the boat for crossing over others.
Selections of Poems on the Lotus Land (Concluded)
